Now, Mr. Speaker, I have intruded somewhat upon the grace of the House in speaking so long. I have spoken in order to indicate the course I intend to take and of which I give the House warning. As occasion presents itself I intend to bring forward these questions and dis-



cuss them. In particular I shall take the first suitable opportunity-I think I will wait until we hear from this delegation from the west-to show to the House that the one fundamental thing in regard to transportation in Canada is to have a definition of our rights under the contract with the Canadian Pacific railway, to order that we may have lower rates, in order to stop these enormous profits, especially to stop this ' melon-cutting ' that has taken place, and to compel that company-and it. is a great company, and I wish to compliment it upon its greatness and upon the excellence of its service in some ways-to respect the rights of the people, to respect the spirit of democracy which is growing strong with us as throughout the world, and to give its main energy to the service of the people.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
MONK (Jacques Cartier) Mr. Speaker, I always listen with some interest to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean), he is so very democratic. He wants the people of all the world to express their will and exercise freely control of their own affairs to which they are entitled-except when it comes to the province of Quebec. In relation to that province his theories change completely. We have a prayer in our church in which enumeration is made of present evils, and the answer of the faithful as each is named, 'O Lord, deliver us!' I think the enumeration is not quite sufficient. I would be inclined to add for this country certain newspapers and their Montreal correspondents well known to us, including the newspaper of my hon. friend. And nobody would answer with more fervour than I. '0 Lord, deliver us!'
I would not, without special reason break a custom which I think, most of us will recognize as a practical and good one, that the speech from the Throne should not be the object of a general debate. That is a custom established in England and marked by few exceptions. However, it , is admitted that under special circumstances the usual formalities are, so to speak, not strictly observed, and the debate is not confined to the mover and seconder of the address and the leaders on either side of the House, but others may take part and new and urgent matters may be considered. It is because I think these urgent circumstances exist that I have taken the liberty of intruding in this debate. I believe these circumstances are imperative. I have looked with interest through this long speech from the Throne. Assuredly nobody in this House will pretend that the subjects there enumerated are not of interest to the House and the country. But there are degrees in this matter. Some of these questions I Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
submit to you and to this House are of a transitory nature. We know, for instance, that we are committed in the construction of the Transcontinental railway, that that construction is progressing and that the cost of it will be enormous. We know that the conditions of trade between ourselves and the British West Indies are being examined by Boyal Commission. We know that we are at present engaged in discussing grave matters with the great republic to the south of us. And this is undoubtedly a matter of great interest. But everybody will admit that such negotiations must frequently take place between countries. Every day throughout Europe you hear of commercial arrangements being made between the countries of that continent. These matters are of frequent occurrence and they are essentially transitory. In the nature of things they are not of the ordinary. It does seem to me and I think it must seem to many people in this House and outside of it that there is a question at present engaging the attention of this country and of the empire which is not of this nature and which dominates in its importance all other questions referred to the speech from the Throne. I need not say to the members of the House that I refer to the policy which has been so extensively discussed during the past year and this year throughout the whole country, which was the subject of most extended debate throughout last session, and which has recently come before the country under circumstances which, it seems to me, render it imperative for this House to take some notice of it. I submit to this House that upon the solution of that question depends the whole future orientation of this country, the direction of our destiny and our relations with the rest of the empire and to a certain extent, with the other nations of the world.
There is no question, I have said it often, and I repeat it as my excuse for taking up the time of this House-there is no question which has come under our consideration since this parliament exists, so momentous, so important as this one. I do think, Sir, that we might have expected in the speech from the Throne something more than we find in it, something more than a commonplace, something more than a mere reference of a passing nature to that great question which is tormenting us at this moment throughout Canada, not in any one province. but throughout the whole country. Sir, when I left this House a year ago we had the impression that the government was going to proceed at once to the execution of the policy which had been laid down by the Prime Minister, and which he had stated in answer to a question which I put to him, namely, the policy defined, initiated and laid down by the Imperial Defence

Conference in 1909. We were to build a navy under agreements we had made at that conference, ships were to be laid down, a naval school was to be established here. The circumstances were urgent, we were to proceed at once to the execution of that policy that had been adopted by the majority of this House after a discussion as violent and as prolonged as any I have heard since I have been a member of this House. Scarcely six lines in regard to it in the speech from the Throne, nothing more as to what has been done since our adjournment:
Negotiations for the acquisition from the Admiralty of the two cruisers ' Niobe ' and ' Rainbow ' have been carried on with His Majesty's government, and the two ships have now arrived and are stationed in Canadian waters, in pursuance of the policy adopted last session for the creation of a naval service.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we were entitled to something more than that to inform us what has been done since the adjournment of this House, and particularly as to what it is intended to do in the future in regard to this matter. I do not for a moment desire to minimize the importance of many of the subjects mentioned in that speech; but it does seem to me that the naval question is even more important than the subject of our negotiations with the United States.
Sir, I was surprised to hear my right hon. friend's statement to this House of what he did in regard to the tariff. During the whole of his trip throughout the west, the further west he went the more affirmative he was as to the utility and urgency of our entering into negotiations with our American neighbours. Did you notice, Mr. Speaker, that as he came east, and finally when he reached Montreal, there came a change over the spirit of his dream, and, so to speak, he withdrew from that position. Last night my right hon. friend told us that the cardinal principle laid down in the Fielding tariff was the British preference. I speak as one who was brought up in the school of Sir John A. Macdonald, and I do not believe that the cardinal policy which should guide this government at present in connection with these negotiations is the British preference. I have approved of that preference. It is true that I have contended in this House, therein echoing, I believe, the opinion of many, that so long as that preference was one-sided it was incomplete. I was only echoing the opinion of the Minister of Finance, at the conference in 1902, stated to the representatives of the British countries, in a memorandum which I believe was presented at that conference, or at the conference of 1907, that if there was no mutuality in the tariff preference, it would be for us to consider whether we
should not make more favourable arrangements with other nations, whether it was not our duty to change the conditions of a favour which we had extended with pleasure in the expectation of reciprocity. But I say that the cardinal principle which should guide us in all matters relating to the tariff is the advantage of Canada, the welfare of our own industrial life. That is the cardinal principle, and I join issue with my right hon. friend in the proposition which he laid down last night, that the British preference was the cardinal principle which should guide us in the negotiations which, it seems to me, have become necessary with our neighbours. Sir, if we take as our guiding principle what was laid down by Sir John A. Macdonald in 1878, the principle to which the Conservative party has ever been faithful, we will accomplish two things:	We
will negotiate with our neighbours upon points upon subjects where our own interests, the interests of our industrial life, are not affected. Why should we not have commercial relations with them? The moment our own interests are at stake and nobody will understand that better than our neighbours themselves-then we can hesitate. But it does seem to me that if by an interchange of commodities, of farm products, and such articles, where we can, without injury to our own people, and where they can, without injury to themselves, but with mutual benefit to both sides, make an exchange, and lessen the burden of a heavy tariff, why should we not accept the invitation now extended to us? I must say that our negotiations and our treaties with our neighbours from the very beginning have not been' of such a nature as to prevent us from viewing with fear the resumption by my right hon. friend and his government of those negotiations.
Mr. Speaker, we have had an election in the province of Quebec which to my mind ought not to be ignored by this House and it is on account of the expression of the popular will of the constituency which m,y right hon. friend opened under circumstances which I shall refer to in a moment, it is on account of the unmistakable manifestation there of what is throughout my own province and as I shall endeavour to show to the House throughout the other provinces of this Dominion, the desire and the will of the people, that I have to-day taken the opportunity of addressing the House in order to submit to yourself and to this House a proposal which I think will commend itself to all people in this House who have some regard to the manifestations of public desires. A certain number of us have found that what we claimed at the last session has been endorsed by the people. At that time a large number of the members of this House were in

favour of submitting to the people a question upon which the people had never been consulted and upon which they claimed and had a right to express an opinion before the government adopted, in a definite way its policy. A very large number of petitioners, this House will remember last year addressed the House from all parts of the country and requested that favour, representing that the people of Canada 'had been afforded no opportunity of expressing their opinion upon this question. For my part during the time of the session that 1 was in the House, I presented petitions from over 9,000 electors who asked for that right, and if I take into consideration the petitions that were presented by other members and for other electors, I think I am within the mark in saying that over 50,000 electors in this country did on that occasion ask the House for a reference of this question to the people for an expression of their opinion.
Let me say a word as to the circumstances under which in the county of Drummond and Arthabaska the people were called upon to express their opinion upon this question. Those who remember something of our political history will bear in mind the period which just preceded the_ fall from power of the government which preceded this one. There were at that time if I mistake not, and I speak from memory, three partial elections in which the government was defeated. If I refer to that distant period it is with the object of drawing attention to the fact that the government at that time was not fearful of consulting the people in constituencies of a doubtful nature. The government went to the people without picking out and chosing a constituency where they had every opportunity of carrying the contest. There was an election in the county of Vercheres, there was an election which the government might have avoided in the county of Jacques Cartier, a most divided county and in the constituency of St. Anne where the same condition existed. Although the government was at that time on the eve of a general election it did not hesitate to go down to those-counties and boldly take the opinion of the people on the question of the day. How different has been the conduct of my right hon. friend, he who spoke last session of the shivering electors in the county of Jacaues Cartier, has not shown in this instance that bravery which he fails to find in other people.
My right hon. friend began on his return from the west by going down to that constituency in the province of Quebec where almost inevitably with the precautions which he was taking he must have felt sure of overcom-Mr. MONK.
ing the little band of the opposition at that time. My right hon. friend, without letting the people at large know that he had decided to open that constituency and to name Mr. Lavergne a senator, went down there and chose his candidate himself, a gentleman whom 1 had the pleasure ol meeting during the campaign, a talented man, speaking both languages fluently; he set to work and began the organization of the election before we had any opportunity of knowing that that constituency was going to be opened. This was a county where, under the most favourable 'circumstances, a conflict is necessarily costly, where my right hon. friend from past experience had reason to believe that it was impossible successfully to contest the election. After the whole organization had taken place Mr. Perrault, the candidate, sought the endorsation of a convention chosen by himself and for attending which each member called received a consideration $4. We became aware of the projected election when these dispositions had been carefully made by my right hon. friend. I am giving these facts without wishing in any way to enhance the result of that election, but I think it is fair to ourselves who carried on that difficult conflict, I think it is just to his House and to the country to make known exactly all facts connected writh it, leaving it to the country to say what importance, what value, what sense is to be attached to the verdict given upon that occasion. Mr. Speaker, there was very much money spent in that election but not on our 3ide.

I have said that we have none of these resources. We invited to the convention by circular, the electors of that Liberal county who took exception to the naval policy of the government. We could not be more frank than that. That was the issue discussed by my hon. friends and myself throughout the province of Quebec during the whole summer, and whatever the difficulties, we wished to face the issue and to test public opinion in the first constituency opened in our province. I attended that convention although I took no part in

the proceedings not being an elector, and that convention was attended by a large number of voters irrespective of party. At that convention, open to the electors in general sharing our opinion, two candidates were nominated. One of them was a young lawyer, a Conservative, a man of talent accustomed to public speaking, and it was suggested that a representative of the agricultural class might be properly selected because the farmers were numerous in the constituency and competent to decide with justice the question which we had raised. Thereupon a farmer-not such a farmer as the Minister of Agriculture but a ile facto farmer, a genuine farmer-thereupon a farmer was put in nomination and he stated that while he always supported the Liberals he differed from them on the question of their naval policy and he was prepared to enter into the conflict upon that issue. The other young gentleman who had been nominated withdrew and the nomination of Mr. Gilbert was made unanimous; and the conflict began. Now, Mr. Speaker, there is just a moment to speak before six o'clock, and I shall refer briefly to the question of our resources. Some difficulty arose last night when I thought that I should interrupt my right hon. friend in the course of his speech which to my mind betrayed a great deal too much ill-humour and petulance, when, the right hon. gentleman made some charges against us as to the conduct of that campaign. I will take the House into my confidence and say that not only were our resources very scant but that we had no money (as I think I need not tell the House and the public), to print pamphlets, and I did not hear of the pamphlet referred to by my right hon. friend until after the election.

speechtext:
I do not say that they did, but who did? We certainly did not. I remember an election in the city of Montreal many years ago in which the late Hon. Thomas White was a candidate. Two days before that election a picture was circulated among the voters showing him in the garb Mr. MONK.
of a Freemason. Mr. White was defeated. Who, on that occasion, circulated that-printed picture? Some of the friends of the right hon. gentleman. What I do say is that if the conflict in Drummond and Arthabaska had not taken place under such terrible disadvantages on our side and against such fearful odds, I believe that our candidate would have been elected by over 2,000 of a majority. HoAvever, as we were absolutely lacking in the means and devices which hon. gentlemen had under their control and so freely used, he got in by a bare majority. But I do not think we ought to rely on isolated utterances or attach too much importance to them. I think it important to show that when I made that statement last night I had grounds for it, and nobody will deny that; but I had not heard Mr. Begin himself, although I heard much argument by our adversaries in that election of the same nature. But without having before one the surrounding circumstances, to pick out a word or a phrase from a discussion does not give a fair criterion of what was said. I would rather in this case rely upon what my right hon. friend himself laid down for the enlightenment of the electors of the province of Quebec as the policy of the government. A few days before that election he came to Montreal. That was immediately following his return from the west. A demonstration was organized in his honour; it was Supposed to be a triumph, but I witnessed that show and was painfully impressed. Here, again, no expense was spared. I have no doubt that at least $10,000 was expended to give my right hon friend a proof of popular favour. There were fire crackers galore, cabs without number and many of them empty, and there were bearers of torches evidently salaried. There could be no doubt about that; one did not require to be a psychologist to see it. And there were bombs which kept the poor inhabitants of that section of Montreal awake most of the night. There was very little genuineness about that reception; it was all outward show. Such was the universal opinion of the people of that city, and I feel convinced that my right hon. friend himself did not feel very comfortable. No doubt he was not at the bottom of that large and insincere expense. Who was? Probably the men who furnished the funds for the election in Drummond and Arthabaska. Well, my right hon. friend came to Montreal and delivered -a long speech, which a large number of salaried stenographers took down and which was printed in ' Le Canada ' the following morning. That is a paper which is supported by the whole of us-I was going to say by the government-but I think the money came out of the funds of the country, and 100,000 copies were printed for circulation. From the utterances of my right hon. friend on that occasion I can take

something which, like the articles of government organs, is not provoked in discussion, not expressed in the fire of repartee, but published after calm consideration, and I would rather judge the attitude of the Liberal party on that occasion by what was said by my right hon. friend. Let us see what reasons he gave the electors of the province of Quebec for the government's naval policy and the construction of this fleet. I am translating from the verbatim report of his speech published in this newspaper:-
Wliat, I say, is the reason we had to propose and vote this navy Bill. Here, gentlemen, is a question upon which superior minds can pronounce and which they can discuss, and I am here to state it to you. The reason why we proposed the navy law in 1910, you will find in the memo. I read to you just now, when I said we proposed to organize a service of naval defence as we increased in population and in wealth.
This law was proposed in 1902, in 1908 and in 1910-only eight years have elapsed since its first proposal. Eight years, gentlemen, is only a moment in the life of a nation, but in that moment Canada has made giant strides towards progress. We are under conditions different from those of 1902. We have increased in population, and we have increased in wealth. Our population has increased more than thirty per cent; our revenue has increased more than one hundred per cent. In 1902, our population, as established by the census, was 5,375,000; in 1910, I have, no hesitation in saying, it is eight millions and over. Our revenue in 1902 was $48,000,000; our revenue now is over $100,000,000; this year it will be more than $112,000,000. Now, gentlemen, these are the reasons, as I stated in the memorandum, why, in 1910, we have accomplished the work which we declared we could not accomplish in 1902. But there is another reason.
And my right hon. friend goes on to give that other reason. I will not quote it at length ; the House can verify what I am stating. That other reason is that we have become a nation and, as a nation, our duty is to defend ourselves. Having, in the interval between 1902 and last year, become a nation, according to my right hon. friend, the duty was imposed upon us to defend ourselves-I presume, by land as well as by sea. Now, is that a faithful and sincere exposition of the question? I consider not. I consider it to be eminently wanting in frankness, truthfulness and sincerity. But that is the position he took in Quebec ; and I call your attention to the fact that, since the election in Drummond and Arthabaska it is the position which the government intends to take throughout the country. Thai position is : We have increased in population and in wealth and are therefore in a position to have a navy; we have become a nation and are therefore obligated to have a navy. Let me give as proof of this a quotation from the government organ.
Speaking upon this point, the Montreal ' Herald ' of the 21st instant gives these reasons for the creation of a navy :
(1)	That the withdrawal of British squadrons from our two seaboards left work to be done which it is the business of Canada as a united, strong and respected nation to do;
(2)	That the withdrawal by Great Britain of her own motion, and her handing over to us the fortifications at Halifax and Esqui-malt was the ' confirmation of our autonomy,' and the demonstration of her confidence in our loyalty and friendship;
(3)	That in taking up the work which thus offers to our hand, we are pursuing the normal course of our national development and are at the same time enabled ' to hold up our heads in the British Empire ';
(4)	That Canada has and should have the power to control its naval service according to the free will of the people as expressed by their responsible rulers.
That is the ground taken to-day by the government throughout the country particularly in the province of Quebec. I think it necessary to point out to the House what was the programme upon which my right hon. friend intended to he judged in the county which he was then about to open. A resolution was moved in this House in November, 1908, by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). Compare these statements which I have just read with the demands of that proposed resolution. 1 will not read the resolution to the House, for I desire to be ibrief. But it was to the effect that the time had arrived for us to see to the protection in an effective way of our coasts, harbours and ports, protection of the country generally. What is the difference, au fond and in reality, between the idea expressed in that resolution and that expressed in the statement of the Prime Minister at Montreal just before the election, and that in this statement of the ' Herald ' which I have just read? Is that in reality what we have had before us who have followed public events since 1902? I say, no. This is not the idea presented to the imperial conference of 1902, the conference of 1907 and finally the imperial defence conference of Julv and August, 1909. I could quote from the documents of the first, the second and the third; but is it necessary to take up the time of the House on such a question? Is it not true that from the very first the new question mooted, admitted by every body to be a new question. was the question of our participation in the defence of the empire? Is there a man in this House who will say that was not the question laid before this great, conference and discussed, with the results with which we are all familiar? At the conference of 1902, to begin with, was not that the question, our participation in the defence of the empire? No longer the old

traditional policy recognized in this country by both parties that we should defend our own country, but the question of more intimate union with the empire and cooperation in its defence. And at that time my right hon. friend-let'us bear in mind- took the ground that he could not accede to that proposition. That was the ground he took, clearly, undoubtedly. And when he returned to Canada he was feted and had a far greater triumph as he came up the River St. Lawrence than that of the other day. All his press lauded him for the attitude he took in that conference. Two years elapsed, and I am not aware that during that time his position was challenged or traversed in this House or in the country. I speak from memory, but I think I am not mistaken. . Yes, I recollect now that my hon. friend, the democrat, the disciple of Demos, the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean), on one occasion called upon the Prime Minister for some explanation upon that question. And we all remember-it has been quoted often enough in the papers since-the indignation with which my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) met the remarks of the hon. member for South York and stated that had he acceded to the proposition made in the conference it would have been suicide and a crime against this country. And then came the conference of 1907 to which my right hon. friend was invited. It was suggested to him that three subjects should be discussed, our commercial, our political, and our military relations with the empire.
To that my right hon. friend answered that he was prepared to discuss commercial relations, but that the political and military relations were satisfactory as they were. He went to the conference, and I will not entertain this House with his attitude there in 1907. Bui in reference to that motion made by Dr. Smartt which I have here, and which laid clearly before the conference a proposal that we should participate in some way or other, either by a contribution in money, or by naval preparations of our own, or by other naval services relieving the Admiralty-we were to do something-my Tight hon. friend became irritated, almost as much irritated as he was last night, and declared that he could not accede to such a proposal, comprehensive as it was, and that if it were submitted to the conference he would have to vote against it. This is a summary of the facts. My right hon. friend came back here, and was greeted in the same way as when he had previously returned, lauded by his own people, and lauded by his own partisans. I am not aware that in the elections of 1908. or at any time-1 speak subject to correction

his conduct in that respect was called into question. How can we explain the attitude of my right hon. friend subse-.

In 1909, on the 10th of February, after having had previously, at the conference of 1907, refused to accede to the proposal of the War Office for a military organization, when the House, I say, was in session, when we were here ready to speak on behalf of the people, an order in council was passed which is quoted in these documents, absolutely approving of the military plans of the War Office, and directing that a telegram should be sent to London in these terms:	__
Your despatch, Canada, 30, of January 15th. My ministers fully accept the principles set forth in memorandum by general staff. Despatch will follow explaining precise position of Dominion government.
Now I would like to ask the House how it is that a plan which had been previously made and had been refused by my right hon, friend,, should, when the House is sitting on the 10th of February, 1909, by an order in council, -without consultation with the House in any way, receive the sanction of the government. I have stated that the exposition made by my right hon. friend of his government's policy at the meeting in Montreal, differed essentially from the plan matured in London at the Colonial Defence Conference. I think that difference clearly appears from the most cursory examination of the blue-book which contains a report of that conference. Look at the words of the Prime Minister of England, the right Hon. Mr. Asquith, when he reported to the House of Commons what the conference had done, and what it had decided. It was called to provide for a plan of defence, not for each individual dependency, but for the British Empire in general. The naval plan submitted there, and accepted by the delegates of this government who went to the conference with written instructions from my right hon. friend, is not a plan for the defence of Canada, it is a plan-we must be frank about it-for our co-operation with the British fleet in the defence of the empire and the maintenance of its supremacy at sea. It was expressly agreed there by our delegates along with all the other delegates, agreed

unanimously, that in case of war our fleet, as well as all the other co-operating units, should fall ipso facto under the control of the British Admiralty for direction during the war. There can be no doubt whatever about that. Can any one contradict that? Will my right hon. friend contradict that statement made by Mr. Asquith, -and contained in. a memorandum of the admiralty and approved by our delegates? What may be written in our own naval law may be something different, I think it is not. War is not a trifling matter. Our policy, if we approve of it, does not rest on a Naval Bill, or on some section thereof. In my view it rests, if we are honourable men, upon the engagement which we make, and as I read that blue-book it is impossible to reach any other conclusion than that we have agreed to build a fleet for the purpose of co-operation in the maintenance of British supremacy by participation in all the wars of the empire. When, in the county of Drummond and Arthabaska, that assertion was made by us, it was contradicted by the speakers for the government. We referred to the statement made in this House, the very frank, clear and unquestionably true statement, made by my hon_. friend whom, I regret to see, is not present, the Minister of Finance. I will not read his statement to the House, but it can be verified.

The naval service, then, is to be a service primarily for the defence of Canada, but not only for the defence of Canada, Under the measure we are proposing we shall have a naval service which is Canadian in time of peace, but which by the very machinery we have provided will unmistakably become imperial whenever the help of Canada is needed for the defence of the empire. And just or unjust, right or wrong, we will be co-operating in that war whenever it occurs.
That statement which I now make can be verified. If it was a Nationalist who made some of these utterances which my right hon. friend regrets so much, at what school was he brought up? Let me give a sample to the House of the kind of campaign which was carried on in 1896 in the newspapers which were established and kept alive by my right hon. friend's party. ' Le Soir ' was a newspaper which was the product of the work and labour of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries at that time. The House will remember that the Conservative government had purchased some rifles,, and listen to this from 1 Le Soir ' of the 18th of June, 1896, just a few days before the election:-
One of the hobbies of old Tupper is imperial federation. Imperial federation means a more intimate alliance between England and her colonies in general and more specially with Canada.
One of the conditions of that alliance would be that in time of war, Canada should be called upon to pay a share of its costs both in men and money.
And, as England is nearly always at war with some one, we would be forced to continually tax ourselves to find the money, and draw lots to furnish the men.
And in return, England would make these droll baronets, or knights of this or commanders of that.
But the people will remain food for powder.
Sir Charles Tupper had hardly returned from England than he began to prepare the means for the realization of his awful project.
England has been threatened with difficulties with the United States regarding a few acres of mining lands of which she claims the property in Venezuela, situated many thou-

sand miles from our country, in Central America. At once, Sir Charles Tupper to make himself officious, orders the purchase in England of rifles and guns, &c., for one million eight hundred thousand dollars ($1,800,000) during the session and without consulting parliament.
But that was not enough.
He must have three millions.

The electors should bear in mind that those big and fat leaders who are always desirous to exhibit themselves as more patriotic than others, more loyal than others and ready to plunge us into war for the benefit of others, will not be the parties who will pay and bear the burden.

I am not aware that any such language as that was ever uttered during our campaign. I stated at every meeting I attended that far from wishing to segregate my province from any other province of the Dominion, I was ready to defend the views which I hold in any' other province, and particularly in Ontario. I stated on many occasions during that campaign, and I state it here, Mr. Speaker, that it is my abiding belief that the people of Ontario (when they are made fully acquainted with all the circumstances of this complicated question which have so far largely been kept hidden from the people) will give a similar verdict to that pronounced by the electors of Drummond-Arthabaska. I have no hesitation in making that statement. I find that these newspapers in Ontario which are uncontrolled and unfettered have expressed that very view. Three of the great agricultural newspapers of that province are my authority for that opinion. I could quote
from newspapers in Ontario and other provinces to show that the verdict given by the electors of Drummond-Arthabaska is a just and fair verdict, and a verdict which may be obtained in any other of the provinces of Canada. There is no desire for segregation. My hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean) has been ill-informed as to the nature of that campaign. He knows nothing whatever of it, and if he has gathered his information from his correspondent in Montreal I can tell him that that information is incorrect and does not truly represent the facts. I state to you now, Mr. Speaker, and I state to this House and to the country that in none of these utterances delivered in the province of Quebec was there even the idea of separation expressed by any of us. No such idea exists in the mind of the people of my province. There is no question of annexation in Quebec. The uniform statement made by those who were arguing this question before the electors in that province was that we were perfectly satisfied with our relations with the mother country as they exist at present. Is not that satisfactory, is there any grumbling in that? Is there any traitorous language about that? Is there anything disloyal about it ? Is not this question which we have so much discussed in this House and elsewhere a very great political public question, which should be discussed by the representatives of the people? And why is it that the newspapers fettered and trammelled and circumvented and controlled will not at least give us the credit of acting in good faith? Will anybody in this House maintain that it is disloyal to discuss such a question? Will any sane man deny that a change in our relations with the empire upon which the people have never had an opportunity to pronounce is a fit subject matter to be discussed by free people? And, Sir, whence have a great many of the people of Ontario sprung? They are largely the descendants of United Empire Loyalists, and we who know the history of these men and all they suffered for their principles, know how they cherished the principle of self-government. The Anglo-Saxon prides himself above all things on the right of self-government, and the question as to whether that right is preserved by this new arrangement is a question which it is fair to discuss. At the conference of 1907, Lord Tweedmouth proposed co-opeTation, and he said:-
If we submit to you to decide for us the question of co-operation, it must be accompanied by representation ; we cannot ask you to become responsible for the empire throughout the world without offering you representation ; Sir Wilfrid Laurier has spoken of representation-and he quoted his words ; well, he said, the question is to determine how that will be provided, but we never would ask you to accept the



burden without the corresponding right of being consulted. Where, then, is the disloyalty of pointing out that in this scheme we become responsible as honourable men taking engagements, for the policy of the British government throughout the empire *without any right to speak provided? Are we, in this country and in the great selfgoverning dependencies prepared to assume such responsibilities as that? Is it not fair to discuss it? If Lord Tweedmouth was right in proposing it in the language in which he did, are we not entitled to consider it without being marked with the infamy of disloyalty? My opinion, Mr. Speaker, of the school of Imperialists is this, that a man should be sincerely and clearly of opinion that the relations of the empire should be changed, that there should be centralization, that this new scheme, such as it is, is a fit and proper one. 1 respect his convictions, but I say this without being-a prophet :	the way in which that
school brands with infamy those who do not share their views is proof to me that those men are perhaps the worst enemies of the British Empire, because they attack the freedom which is the birthright of every British subject ; and if they persist in that course, which forbids free discussion such as we have a right to as born British subjects, they will ultimately work friction and disaffection among well-intentioned and loyal men. Well, Sir, in the campaign in Quebec there was' no disaffection, no complaint of our present relations, but, a fair and open discussion of the change proposed, nothing more. Were the orators who spoke at those meetings prepared to forswear the principle which has obtained in this country for all time, and which has been admitted and recognized by both parties at all times, that we are bound to defend our own country? Never, Sir, under any circumstances. When the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Brodeur), who made a short appearance and to me a very painful one on the nomination day, spoke of the men who were discussing this question as men who were afraid to defend their country, he knew that he was saying what was unfair to the inhabitants of the province of Quebec since we have been under the British flag, and tearing to pieces the most glorious part of Canadian history. We have never for a moment contradicted that principle. It was laid down by both parties. Cartier, Macdonald, Dorion, Sir Charles Tupper himself, have at all times maintained that principle ; and when my hon. friend the Minister of Marine spoke at the Imperial conference of 1907, he stated, as one of his reasons for dissenting from the plan which was submitted to the conference, that both parties in this country had always held this and nothing else, that we were bound, not only in principle, Mr. MONK.
but by special arrangement with the British government, of which proof abundant is not wanting to undertake the defence of our country and our shores, and to maintain in this country the honour of the British flag, the supremacy of England. There has been no discussion upon that on our side in any degree. Therefore it is a calumny which it is time to stop, to say that the men of the school to which I belong in my province and elsewhere are -not prepared to maintain that principle 75 years old or more, established by arrangement with the British government. I alluded last year to what had been matured in England by a special committee of the English Privy Council-a plan of defence,
I hope we shall have before the House in a few days-the sum-total of the wisdom of imperial statesmen during the Victorian period. The House will find, as we know from an authentic declaration of the Duke of Devonshire in the House of Lords, that that scheme was limited to the defence of Canada by ourselves, and the placing of certain ports in this country at the disposal of the British fleet. The government of England was satisfied that we should undertake that as our share in the defence of the empire. Why should we to-day be stopped from discussing a new and different scheme which has never emanated from the British government itself?
Mr. Speaker, I wish to abridge. We have been taxed with wandering from the principles of the Conservative party, those of us who in this instance have seen fit not to agree exactly with other members of the party. I do not wish to enter at length into that question ; but it is a question worth studying, We in the province of Quebec are the traditional successors of that party which was founded 50 years ago bearing the name of Liberal-Conservative -Why? Because it was formed by the good-will of eminent men in those days -belonging to both parties, who wanted to put the country at rest and -peace, and who laid down some principles to which, I submit, we have faithfully adhered. Those principles are well known. At the very foundation of those principles was the idea that we were to enjoy in this country the fullest autonomy possible-autonomy in municipal and provincial matters ; and in the confederation, the foundations of which were laid in the city of Quebec at the conference of 1864, the dominant idea was that we should enjoy the utmost autonomy possible, consistent of course with our allegiance to the British crown and the maintenance of the links which bind us to the crown. Cartier's great boast was that he had brought into our country absolute autonomy in municipal matters. The boast of the Conservative party was that it had secured for us the largest possible measure

of autonomy in provincial and federal matters.
There was another principle which was at the root of the arrangement arrived at in Quebec. That was respect for the principle that the father has absolute control, by the superior laws of nature, over the education of his children. That is a principle respected in England to the present day and which _ was introduced into the covenant of our new constitution.
There was also the principle of the development of our natural resources and a policy absolutely Canadian and national. I submit that it is we who have remained strictly faithful to those principles and when I read in the papers that certain members of the Conservative party wish to have the men who hold the views we do ignominiously read out of that party, I ask myself whether it is not absolutely true that it is we who are faithful to the principles advocated by Lafontaine, Morin and the men of Upper Canada who at that time joined hands with them-the principles advocated by Macdonald and Cartier.
What we have claimed is merely a consultation of the people, the right of the people to pronounce upon this vast change upon which they have never been consulted. Under the circumstances I have detailed we went down to the province of Quebec, and in a county selected by my right hon. friend we went before the people. We had a candidate who absolutely upheld our views, and with every possible odds against us we succeeded in gaining a victory on that great question. Was it possible then for us, on reading this insignificant reference in the speech from the Throne to a question of this magnitude, not to take notice of it. Had we failed to do so we would have failed in our duty to the electors. Therefore I have occupied the time of the House, and now beg to move to add the following words to the address.
The House regrets that the speech from the Throne gives no indication whatever of the intention of the government to consult the people on its naval policy and the general question of the contribution of Canada to imperial armaments. I
I regret very much that I have not been able to abridge my remarks. Will you allow me, Sir, to add a point which I failed to bring to the notice of the House. I have not had occasion to speak very often outside the counties of Drummond and Arthabaska to English speaking electors. But I have every reason to believe, from the reception I received there and the result obtained, that this question should be discussed before them. I was invited to speak at a meeting of the Young Men's Christian Association in Montreal immediately after the election. I accepted that invitation and spoke before a select body of English speak-5i
ing men, young and old, deeply interested in the welfare of this country and well qualified to appreciate the arguments I offered. I was thanked by that meeting. I was seen individually by those who had followed that conference and told that although, on all points they did not agree with me, they were of opinion that the arguments, I gave were fair and just, contained no appeal to prejudice, and were suitable to submit to English speaking electors. I represent myself a county in which I am proud to count a very preponderating English vote. I have not had occasion to address the electors of that county at any length, but I am in their hands and am prepared to go before them and repeat what I said to the Young Men's Christian Association. I am prepared to repeat before them what my friends Mr. Bourassa and Mr. Lavergne and the other gentlemen who were with us during that campaign said to the people. I have confidence in the Anglo Saxon spirit of justice and fairness. After all my right hon. friend cannot refute this statement that under this new arrangement it is not to the Crown of England that we become subject but we become the slaves of the English electorate.

speechtext: That is what we become. In a most important part of our national life -our relations with foreign countries, our wars, if war should be a necessity-in all these things we shall be controlled by men elected by the English voters in the British Isles and not elected by ourselves. Anglo-Saxons will not, I believe, accept that condition of affairs. They are not prepared to submit to what must appear to them, more than to us in the province of Quebec, a thraldom to which centuries of freedom have not accustomed them.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Mx. Speaker, I do not know whether it will be possible for me to deal with all the points which my hon/ friend from Jacques Cartier (Mx. Monk) has made in the long speech which he has just delivered. I will try, however, to deal with as many of them as possible in the time at my disposal. I ask to be permitted, at the outset, to congratulate particularly the seconder of the address, the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) on the admirable speech which he delivered yesterday. Unfortunately, that speech was not understood by all the members of the House. I am extremely sorry for that, because it was a most patriotic and most able speech. I hope that, when it is translated into the language of the majority, that speech will be read by all, in order that it may be understood by all, that in the Liberal party there is only one policy on the question of naval defence. I would also offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiverin), but as he has already received from all those who have spoken cordial tributes to his ability, my words will he of no great value under the circumstances.
I am disappointed to find that this question of the naval service is not treated in the patriotic way in which it should be treated by all the members, of this community, and especially by some members of this House. It is very much to be regretted that the programme which, for my part, I enunciated when I came back from the conference in 1909 has not been followed by all. I stated then that, so long as I had anything to do with the naval affairs of this country I would see that the administration thereof would be conducted on lines of patriotism, and that my decisions on questions coming before me should not he affected by party or selfish interests. And, in the administration of the new department of naval service, since it has been organized, whether in the selection of the cadets who wish to enter the navy, in the selection of the physicians, or in the selection of the officers, no party interest has, in any way, shape, or form, guided my decisions, but in all cases we have chosen the officers who were deemed best fitted to perform the duties expected of them. I have put at the head of the 'Niobe' the son of a Conservative, a respected senator of this parliament. I have put at the head of the ' Rainbow,' on the Pacific ocean, a man who has no political affiliations so far as I know and who is connected with a Con-Mr. MONK.
servative family. I have carried out this policy because I desire that this question of naval defence should be not _ a party question, but a Canadian and national question. I am extremely sorry to find that our opponents do not seem to realize the importance of raising this question above the level of party politics. Look at England, our mother country. Do we find there that the question of naval defence or military defence is made a question of party warfare? No; they are too patriotic for that. In 1909, every one in this House, Conservatives and Liberals, joined hands to give this country, the mother country, and the world to understand that we were all united in favour of providing for our defence, and for our share of the defence of the empire. I am sorry to know that, a short time after this patriotic movement was unanimously begun, the Conservative party, in order to gain a political advantage, tried to treat this question according to the requirements of party exigencies. And they have not been satisfied even with that state of affairs. They thought advisable, in their interests, to raise a racial issue. In Ontario they denounced the government in stating that our policy was antiBritish, while at the same time the same party in the province of Quebec was carrying on a war against the Liberal party as being pro-British, and too much in favour of England. That, is a situation which, for my part, I denounce. I am sorry that our oponents have not been willing to follow the example which I myself have shown in the administration of my department, of judging every question involved on patriotic grounds, and that they seek party advantage even in a question so vitally important to the interest of the country. I will not speak much today of the movement they have started in Ontario, but will refer particularly to what they have been doing in the province of Quebec. In that province, for several months past, they have tried to raise feeling against this government on the ground that this government wanted to sacrifice every body in favour of Great Britain. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier and his friends have been trying by every possible means to arouse popular prejudices.
He stated a moment ago in his speech that he had been very badly treated by the government, because he did not get French copies of the documents containing the proceedings of the conference of 1909. Of course, this statement of his will be scattered tomorrow over the province of Quebec, and we shall see some of the newspapers supporting him publishing the statement of my hon. friend that once more the French language has been sacrificed by this government in refusing to supply my hon. friend with French copies of "that document. This is the kind of warfare that is being carried on in our province. I will
NOVEMBEK 22,_ 1910
now read a copy of a letter which -was sent on the 18th of August to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, which I hope will be reproduced by those papers which are carrying on this warfare.
F. D. Monk, M.P.,
Montreal, Que.
Replying to your telegram of this date I beg to advise you that I am forwarding you 50 copies of the Naval Act of last session in French.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows very well that the printing of all documents laid on the table of this House is dependent upon the decision of the Joint Committee on Printing. I am not a member of that committee, but I see that my hon. friend for Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel) is a member of that committee, and I now ask the hon. member for Terrebonne why he did not make it his duty as a member of that committee to have this document printed. M,y hon. friend from Jacques Cartier is trying to throw blame upon the government. Here is another letter which was sent by the King's Printer to my hon. friend on the 30th of September and which indicates that this officer who is an officer of the government had nothing to do with the distribution of that report:
in a position to let you have copies of the blue-book relating to the Imperial Defence Conference, 1909. This report was printed by order of parliament and no extra copies were kept at the Bureau. Possibly Mr. Davidson, of the House of Commons Distribution Office, may be in a position to meet your wishes.
I say, therefore, it is unfair for my hon. friend to try to hold the government responsible in relation to this matter. The printing of this document is entirely in the hands of the House of Commons and of the Senate, and is one with which the government has nothing to do.
Now, Sir, my hon. friend has referred to the election in Drummond-Arthabaska, and he has given us a lot of details about the organization and about the voting at that election. He says they had no money and no whisky. My information is to the contrary. I am informed that there was a great deal of money and a great deal of "whisky. There was, moreover, something much more serious, and that is the kind of campaign that "was waged by the friends of my hon. friend. My hon. friend has been like myself, not much in the county; he did not hold many meetings there. But his friends did hold many meetings there, and he says he will retract nothing of what was said by his friends in his presence.
But before coming to the election in Drummond-Arthabaska I may mention some statements that were made, if I am correctly informed, in the presence of my hon. friend at other meetings held during last summer. The first meeting which was held bv the friends of mv hon. friend was in the village of St. Eustache. I have here a statement which I took from the 'Devoir', a newspaper in which my hon. friend writes occasionally, and this declaration was made in the presence of my hon. friend. I will read it, and perhaps my hon. friend will remember some of the pretty warm declarations that were made by his ally. Ought I to say his ally? Should-1 not rather say his leader? Some say that this gentleman is my hon. friend's leader. At one time my friend was willing to stand for a policy affirming the necessity of maintaining the naval supremacy of Great Britain and to follow the course which he followed in 1900 after the South African war.
I suppose my hon. friend has not forgotten the noble position he then took, for fear he might have forgotten I will read the patriotic declarations made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier in 1900. He was answering the gentleman who, for the moment. I will call his ally.

His chief.
Dear Mr. Monk,-I beg to acknowledge re- Mr. BRODEUR. Say his chief if you like, ceipt of your esteemed favour of a recent Here is what the hon. member for Jacques date and in reply regret to say that I am not I Cartier said, and it is pretty good stuff:-

I venture to say tliere are very few French members who sit in this House whose relatives have not at some time had occasion to prove that devotion (to the British Empire). Well under these circumstances, is it not time that the system of playing upon the sentiments of the people for party purposes, should be done away with, and that we should learn to discuss and to examine political questions upon their true merits.
For my part, I am willing to go down to my county where the majority are Frenchspeaking, and am willing to trust myself to their judgment respecting the attitude we have thought fit to take up on this side of the House in regard to this question. I am prepared to go down before the people of my county and take the position that it would have been disastrous for us, when every other part of the empire saw fit to take part in this struggle, it would have placed us in a most humiliating position, if we had not done so ourselves. I am prepared to put that fairly before them. I am prepared to go before the people of my county and expose to them what would have been our position if we had failed to take that share in the defence of the empire which every other colony has seen fit to take.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
The member for Jacques Cartier said that. He added also:
I must confess to you, Sir, that the day before yesterday when, on leaving my room, I saw the flag at half mast upon this building, and heard the news that so many of our fellow-countrymen had fallen in defence of that flag in South Africa, I must confess to you that any hesitation I may have had promptly disappeared. I think it is time for us fully to realize what our position is in this great empire, and having realized that position, to assume all the responsibilities which it involves.	i	| I I
I commend this language of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier of 1900 to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier of 1910. Lately he fell in bad company and that is what- brought the change. He saw that the member for Labelle, with his appeals to prejudice, could influence many people in the province of Quebec, and so could help his party. He went to him and said: Well, now, let us form an association. Probably before going there he went to see some of his friends in Ontario and said to them: Now my friends, do not be scared, I am going to Quebec, I am going to see my friend Bourassa, and make an alliance with him. Now go in your province, denounce Laurier because he is anti-British, I am going into Quebec to make a contrary campaign. The conspiracy has been organized in that way and is now in full operation. My hon. friend stated in Drummond and Arthabaska that he had separated from his party-yes on the lips he has separated from his party, but in the heart he is still a Mr. BRODEUR.
Conservative and to-day is fighting the fights of his party.
My hon. friend stated a few minutes ago that he would stand by the declarations which have been made in his presence. Well, here is one from Mr. Bourassa, at St. Eustache on the 17th of July at which the hon. member was present. On that occasion Mr. Bourassa said.
Then, again, when big ships will have replaced small ships, and when we will have gone in that disastrous policy of which Laurier and Borden are the prophets, when this policy will have fully developed, one day conscription will be enforced, and this little lad here that you send to school to study the law of God as well as that of man so that he may take your place to continue to fecundate the old farm where you were born, where you have learned, in the furrows made by your forefathers, to be Catholics, to be Canadians, to respect law and to nobly accomplish your duty, then this little child, if you should continue to listen to Mr. Laurier, this little child taken away and put under arms, embarked on the fleet of which you will have approved, this little child, I say, who will shed his blood on a foreign land, disembowelled by a Chinese or a Japanese cannon ball, he will have a right to curse you, if you were to sacrifice to the partisanship which binds you to one man, your duty as a citizen and as a free man.
Now Mr. Speaker, I understand that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier stands for that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
That is the kind of campaign these people carried on. Mr. Des-carrie, an elector of my hon. friend, followed and explained how the new Act was a danger for the French Canadian race.
Now we come to a meeting at Farnham before the election. On September 19, Mr. Bourassa said, speaking of Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
It is all very well for him; he has no children. Ten years hence or perhaps sooner, he will have disappeared from the scene of politics. For fifteen years he has trodden on everything sacred to his compatriots in order to make a pedestal for the English who distribute the titles, medals and decorations.
My hon. friend stands for that.
Perhaps we men of to-day will not suffer very much from such a policy, but you, heads of families, old men who have one foot in the grave, you perhaps will be asleep in death before the disastrous effects of this ignominious policy are felt, but you have children. I see some in this meeting who smile over the future of their country. They are eight or ten years old. They were brought up on the knees of their mothers and they count on you to protect them from all the dangers which may reach them, but when, 15 years hence, you heads of families will not be any longer here-but your wives may still be here-when 15 years hence your wives will see the agent of the government, having in his hands this accursed Act, and addressing each one of them, he will say: ' Good mother, thou must give thy sons not to defend their native soil, but to fight on all the lands and seas of the world on behalf of the English flag/ Then, when your wives will learn some months later that an Austrian shell, a Japanese cannon ball, or a German bullet, will have disembowelled their children, and that they have fallen over precipices, or collapsed on the deck of a ship, do you think they will then say:
' Very well, my husband was rouge, and it is Mr. Laurier who passed the Act. He did well/
No, they will curse you, and it will be only right.
At Grand-Mere also a meeting was held, in the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Champlain. I quote from Mr. Bourassa:
Mr. Laurier has betrayed the province of Quebec and Canada, but he will not live to see the consequences of his iniquitous act. Mr. Laurier is 70 years of age, and has no children. He does not care about the consequences, but we who have founded homes, we who know what the birth of a child costs, and the suffering it brings to the heart and the womb of a mother-we will suffer, and we do suffer in thinking over the future in sight for our sons. The little children who listen to my words this moment, and who smile at the foot of this platform, do not yet understand all that is frightful for them in this iniquitous law of la marine de guerre, but twenty years hence, when the recruiting agent will knock at their doors, and speaking to the mother, will say:
' Mother, thou wast relying on thy child to be the joy and happiness of thine old days; thou wast relying on him to protect thee in thine old age; thou wast relying on his young heart to warm up thine, which is worn by the hard work and grief of a whole life. Thou wast wrong. The Act passed in 1910 by the Laurier government takes away thy children from thee, and thy son must come away with me/
Twenty years hence, perhaps, on the deck of a warship will lie the shattered bowels of your children because you, fathers here, have been too rouge to vote against Laurier.
In that speech he was not referring to any future legislation, but he was stating that conscription was compulsory under what he called the cursed Act of 1910. The member for L'Islet (Mr. Paquet) was present at that meeting.

speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called, I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) to a matter concerning the operation of the Immigration Act and the Alien Labour Act. I see in a Winnipeg paper of a recent date an article, giving names and dates, and relating to the matter I refer to. A Mr. E. F. Hutchings, a manufacturer of harness, in order to meet the requirements of his growing trade, has erected a factory within the last year which cost him $100,000, and he requires 100 trained and expert men to man that factory. The Alien Labour Act prevents him from getting these men from the United States; he had, therefore, to send his agents to the old country to find the men there. The business there is quiet, because the automobile is driving horses out of the market, and many operators there are idle. He finds himself up against this proposition. He says,-I am stating now, repeating now, what I find in the papers-that it is necessary for him to employ men with families, as they are more likely to be permanent. But he finds that it will be necessary for him to advance, not only the passage money, but the $50 which every immigrant must have in his pocket before he can land on the shores of Canada. It is stated, further in this paper, that Mr. Hutchings is willing to do that, but that by so doing he would render himself liable to ' a penalty if he advanced $5,000 to these 100

expert men to enable them, to land on this side. I would ask the Minister of the Interior if this matter has been brought to his attention?

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have seen the article in the paper in question, that is to say, the Winnipeg ' Tribune,' giving the details as my hon. friend has placed them before the House. The newspaper has been seriously misinformed in regard to that matter. If Mr. Hutchings or anybody else chooses to advance money to the workmen whom he requires, sufficient to enable them to meet the requirements of the immigration law, there is no objection to his doing so, either as a matter of law or of policy. For the further information of the House, I may mention that the requirement of a sum of money on the part of the immigrant has been a part of the law of Canada for several years, and was made a part of that law for what appeared to be good and sufficient reasons. One reason was that when a man came to this country, which would be to him a strange country, it was desirable that he should have some resources of his own upon which to depend until he was able to procure regular employment. This requirement has not been insisted upon in the cases of men coming to Canada as farm labourers, of women coming as domestic servants, or of persons coming to their relatives already residing in Canada. But in the case_ of other immigrants who did not come within these categories, there has been, since the fall of 1907, a requirement of that kind. Speaking generally, $25 is required during the summer and $50 during the winter, the idea being that if it was right and proper that an immigrant should have $25 on his arrival in summer, when work was plentiful, he should at least have double that amount on his arrival in the winter time, when work is not so plentiful , and employment is more precarious. However, as bearing on this particular case, and as showing how far astray that newspaper is from the truth, I may mention that under the provisions of the Immigration Act passed by parliament last session, which allows the admission of an immigrant by special agreement, it was arranged some time during the summer, in view of the fact that there was a general demand for labour, and that the labour conditions were buoyant, that in the case of men coming to assured employment, if notice was given to the officers of the department on the other side of the water, they should issue a permission to enable the immigrant to land on this side, coming, as I say, to assured employment, even though he had not the money qualification. It has not been considered desirable that this arrangement should be continued during the winter months. But that arrangement is still in force, and will be in force until the 10th Mr. A. HAGGART.
of December. So my hon. friend and the House will see how far aside from the facts the newspaper in question has gone in dealing with this case. The employer in question, or any other employer, by making arrangements in due course, may secure the admission of his workmen at any time before the 10th of December, on the terms I have set forth.

Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned last night I had been quoting some extracts from speeches, newspaper articles and cartoons made by Nationalists and Conservatives in the last campaign in Quebec, and I had also quoted some statements which had been made on and after the election in Drummond-Artha-baska. I was proceeding to show what had been said after the election by some of those Nationalist and Conservative orators. However, before I go on to make any more quotations from those speeches, I may mention to the Hous.e that I hold in my hand a reproduction of almost all the important speeches which were made on the occasions referred to; but I do not want to weary the House by reading those quotations. There are enough, I think, to justify the statement which I made at the outset of my remarks, that our opponents have been carrying on this campaign by making the most incendiary, anti-British appeals against the government and especially against the Prime Minister. May I be permitted just to give another one?-an extract from a speech made by a man who, during the last campaign in Drummond and Artbabaska, accompanied the Conservative, or Nationalist candidate during the whole campaign-Mr. Tancrede Marcil. He spoke at St. Louis de Blandford on the 2nd November, 1910-as you see, Mr. Speaker, it is not so long ago- and on that occasion he said:-
That he was born in the village of St. Eustache, where the English went so far as to desecrate the church in riddling it with bullets and in making their horses drink in the sacred vessels; and that it was for the same English that Laurier was wishing to send them to fight and to be killed.

We see that the same war is going on, that the same Mr. Marcil went up to a meeting two days ago in the county of my hon. friend frofn Bagot (Mr. Marcile) and he spoke as follows.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries

speechtext:
Mr. TancrMe Marcil. Here is a report which I extract from the ' Citizen ' in Ottawa :
Mr. Tancrede Marcil appeared as the champion of Nationalism. He accused the Governor General of having been the creature of Cecil Rhodes who was to have left him several millions. He spoke of children being torn from their mothers' arms to serve on warships and declared that French Canadians were not ready to break their backs for Britain.
This is the campaign which is still going on. Further, I see in this last a reference to His Excellency the Governor General. In view of the charges which have been made at different occasions by the Nationalists Conservatives against him here I may be permitted to state that amongst all the Governors General we have had in Canada there never has been a man who was more devoted to our country or has served it better. He has taken an interest in all our relations, foreign and internal. He has been zealous for the upbuilding of our country. He has visited, at great discomfort to himself, the distant parts of this country and even the wild parts in order to be better informed as to its resources and wealth. Now, I see that they are abusing him in the province of Quebec. I say it is a shame to see such terms used and such charges made in the province of Quebec against the Governor General. It was Lord Grey who some years ago was the one who made possible the celebration of the Tercentenary of the foundation of the old city of Quebec, the cradle of the French Canadian race, and just now we know that His Excellency is exerting all the means at his disposal to secure the erection of a statue to a distinguished heroine of French Canadian extraction, who, in 1692, at the age of 18 years, saved this country from invasion on the part of the Indians. I refer to Mile, de Vercheres. That is what His Excellency the Governor General is doing, and I say that French Canadians who are trying in the province of Quebec to raise prejudice against him are
ungrateful and do not represent the feeling and sentiment of my province.
But, these racial appeals, which have been made by the Conservatives, have not been made exclusively in the province of Quebec, but in the province of Ontario a similar racial campaign was carried on. As we know very well, our naval policy has been denounced in Ontario as being anti-British. In Quebec we axe being denounced because it is a pro-British policy. Let me quote you an article in the ' Mail and Empire,' which has striven by all means possible, as I shall prove in a few minutes, to convince its readers that the policy we are enunciating is not a sound policy for the empire. Here is what the ' Mail and Empire ' of the 24th October, 1910, said, speaking of the speech which I had made in Halifax when the ' Niobe ' was welcomed by me :

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
That is the title of the article.
Significant was the speech of Mr. Brodeur, the First Lord of the Admiralty, at the ceremony which marked the arrival of the ' Niobe ' at Halifax. In that deliverance Mr. Brodeur laid down the principle which governs the navy we are creating. The ships, he declared, are for but one purpose, the coast defence of Canada. They will patrol the Atlantic and Pacific shores and drive off any enemy that may be contemplating an attack upon us. In this way, and in this way alone, will they serve the British Empire.
Now, this same newspaper, on the 22nd of October, just a few days previous, published the speech which I made in Halifax, and I am going to quote from the ' Mail ' extracts of my speech which will show you whether there was anything in that speech which would justify what has been said by the ' Mail and Empire.' Here is the report of my speech as it is reproduced in the ' Mail ' itself. If it had been reproduced in some other paper I could understand that probably they would not have seen it, but here is the extract of the ' Mail and Empire ' itself. Describing the arrival of the ' Niobe ', it said :
It proclaims to the whole British Empire that Canada is willing and proud to provide, as rapidly as circumstances will permit, for her local naval defence and to safeguard her share in the commerce and trade of the empire.
Let me read further:
We must consider that our interests are so interwoven with those of Great Britain that her supremacy on the sea and perpetual command of the great commerce of the world appeals to us to awaken a responsive echo in our country. If then we can assist even in a small way, but in proportion to our strength and resources, to the solidifying of Britain's power, the maintaining of her influence and the safeguarding of her supremacy, it becomes our duty to do so.
