I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, what reliance can be placed on, or what importance can be attached to the utterances of a newspaper which, after having published a speech such as that from which I have read extracts, is now stating that Brodeur simply declared that he was for the coast defence of Canada, especially when we all know that I said, not only in Halifax, but also in the province of Quebec, in the presence of the men who are denouncing me as being too British-when I said there what I say now, that it will always be our duty to stand for the defence and the solidifying of the British Empire.
Yesterday there was a short exchange of words between myself and the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). I asserted that my hon. friend had advised the electors of Drummond and Arthabaska to vote against Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The hon. gentleman did not absolutely deny my statement, but said: Bead over the telegram; see what it is. Well, I am going to read, not only that telegram, but some others which were exchanged between the Montreal ' Herald ' and leaders of the Conservative party. The following telegram was addressed to about 15 leaders of that party by the Montreal organ.
Please reply by wire, collect. How do you advise Conservatives to vote in Arthabaska election ?
Let me first-a tout seigneur, tout hon-neur-quote my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. He simply replied: 'Vote according to your conscience '.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
M-r. BRODEUR. My hon. friend would not stand for those denunciations, those anti-British denunciations, which were being made in the province of Quebec. There is another Conservative leader who was also asked to give his opinion-Mr. Robert Rogers, of Manitoba. Mr. Rogers is one of those who are waving in Manitoba the British flag against this government. Here is what he said:
Every Conservative and loyal Canadian

Mark you, loyal Canadian

-whether in Arthabaska or elsewhere should recognize that his first duty to his country is to vote against the Laurier administration.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. McBride was consulted. Mr. McBride, who is a very shrewd man simply replied: Let Conservatives follow the advice of our leader at Ottawa.
I shall now quote the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Snroule). He replied to the Montreal ' Herald ': I
I have no advice to give. The electors must make their own choice.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries

speechtext: I do not aspire to that honour.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Here is what my hon. friend said in his telegram:
My advice to every Conservative is to vote as his intelligence and conscience dictates.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
But that is not all. Here is more:
The Laurier administration is so extravagant, corrupt and lacking in principle, that I would vote every time to turn it out and eo give opportunity to replace it by a better one.
This was sent during the Drummond election. My hon. friend was urging the good Tories in Drummond and Arthabaska, who might read his telegram, to vote for the defeat of this government. And in so doing, he was supporting Mr. Bourassa. But Mr. Bourassa was singing one song in Quebec, while my hon. friend was singing another in Ontario. That, however, is not all. After the election my hon. friend held a meeting in his constituency, and there he said something about his friend Bourassa. Here is a quotation from what he said, which I find in the ' Citizen ' of the 5th of November last, and my hon. friend will tell me whether it is right or not:

Foster dealt with the question of reciprocity and offered an explanation of the result in Drummond-Arth-abaska making a strong attack upon Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whom he denounced as an autocrat, a wielder of tyrannical power, but who had had his Waterloo and deserved no sympathy. Let us be fair to Bourassa, there is good stuff in him.
Yes, said the hon. gentleman, do not my good friends in Ontario, try to kill this little Bourassa, there is good stuff in

him; let us preserve him in order to overthrow the Liberal government and crush the Prime Minister. The hon. gentleman was not alone of that opinion. Now, he was not alone of that opinion. Another gentleman in Toronto, Mr. Edmond Bristol, a member of this House, said: ' I take this from the Toronto 'World1 of the 8th of Nov.-defended Bourassa and Monk, saying that he did not think they were traitors to the British Empire; he knew them both, and knew their personal opinions.' Their personal opinions! Yes. That shows, Mr. Speaker, the entente cordiale which exists between the Conservatives of Ontario and the Nationalists of Quebec. The hon. member for Centre Toronto advises his friends in Ontario: Do not be afraid of Bourassa; I know his personal opinions. Don't mind what he says in Quebec; I know how his heart really feels. It is suggested, Mr. Speaker, that I should read a telegram which the ex-whip of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Geo. Taylor) sent on the evening of the election to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. That telegram was as follows:-
Accept heartiest congratulations on your great fight and success.
Yes, congratulations, on that great fight, in which the allies of the member of Jacques Cartier and himself were denouncing the Liberal naval policy. Yes, a great fight, when our brothers and mothers and sisters were called on to prevent their sons shedding their blood in the defence of Great Britain. A great fight! Yes, when French Canadians were told that they should not have their backbones smashed for the English. A great fight! when it was said that the navy was a conspiracy of the British to drown French Canadians, and when it wa3 declared that we have had enough of England and the English.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it has been said that there was corruption in Drummond and Arthabaska. Yes, there was, and it was on the other side. Who organized that fight, and who are the men who provided money for it? If my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) were here, perhaps he could give us some explanation of where the money came from. Mr. Thos. Chase Casgrain, a Conservative and ex-member of this House, might give us some explanation as to the money used in that election. The hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Forget), who I regret to see is not in his seat, might also give us some information as to the amount of money used in that election. Mr. Speaker, there was no money improperly used on our side. I appeal to the members who assisted us in that election-and most of my colleagues from the province of Quebec did so-to state in this House if any
one of them went there with money for the election. They went to fight for the interests of the country. They went to assist in putting a -stop to a dangerous agitation which had been going on there for months. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier stated that there was enough whisky in the county to float the ' Niobe ' and the ' Rainbow.' In answer to that I may appeal to the testimony of two members of this House, the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe), and the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay (Mr. Girard). The hon. member for Chicoutimi heard a Conservative and Nationalist organizer asking for a large number of gallons of whisky. The hon. member for Kamouraska could also give us evidence on that point.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I will not discuss any longer these racial appeals,, which have been made, not only in the province! of Quebec, but also in the other provinces, in the discussion of this naval policy. I am sorry to say that we have too many of these racial and religious appeals in this country. I observe that the Conservatives. and Nationalists are going to carry on a religious campaign in this House this session. One member of this House, who rides the Protestant horse, is asking whether guards of honour were placed at the disposal of His Eminence Cardinal Vannutelli when he came to attend the Eucharistic Congress some time ago. In the Senate you have the other side of the question. There Senator Landry is trying to cast some blame on the government because we did not pro-! vide guards of honour for His Eminence. I might perhaps read these two questions. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is asking this:

1.	On what occasions and for whom may guards of honour be furnished from the Canadian permanent forces?
2.	By whose authority may they be so furnished?
3.	On what occasions were guards of honour furnished, from the force, at Quebec, Three Rivers and Montreal during the present year, and by whose direction and under whose authority were they so furnished?
i. Did the 65th Battalion, of Montreal, parade at the Eucharistic Congress during the carrying of the Host? and if so, were they equipped with rifles and bayonets? If so, by whose authority?
I rise to a point of order. Can the hon. member anticipate matters on the Order Paper.

motion or declaration or document which may be the subject of an order of the day. I am not quoting from an order of the day, but simply a notice of a question, and I think I am within my rights in quoting it. However, I wish to submit myself to the judgment of the Speaker on that point.

speechtext: Do I understand .you, Mr. Speaker, to say that I am out of order in quoting this?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
May I be permitted to show the reverse of the medal. The Hon. Mr. Landry has put the following motion on the Order Paper of the Senate:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General, praying that His Excellency will cause to be laid before the Senate, copies of all orders in council, of all decisions rendered by the Military Council or some of its members, and of all correspondence concerning the guard and escort of honour applied for in August and September last on the occasion of the visit in Quebec and Montreal of His Eminence Cardinal Vannutelli.
In citing these notices of motions I want to show that it is very unfortunate that we cannot avoid racial and religious appeals in this country. Should such appeals not be stopped? Is it not the duty of every good citizen of Canada to endeavour to put an end to them? No political party can reap advantage from them. These appeals do not count for much among political partisans, but the unfortunate part of it is that there are some people in the country whose minds are influenced by them. Take my own case. Only a few days ago it was stated in some Ontario Conservative newspapers that the Department of the Naval Service should not be under the control of a French Canadian. Is it not unfair -and unjust to make such a statement. I think, Mr. Speaker, I have given to my countrymen sufficient example of devotion and loyalty to be free from any such allegation. And, in speaking of these racial appeals I do not wish to be understood as saying that they are confined to one party only. Unfortunately, occasionally racial and religious appeals are made on both sides, but h-as not the time arrived when all good Canadians should unite to put an end to such an unworthy state of affairs? Is it not time that Mr. BRODEUR.
racial and religious appeals should cease and that all Canadians should work together for the prosperity and progress of our country?
May I now say a word or two on the motion which has been introduced by my hon. friend (Mr. Monk), and in which regret is expressed that the speech from the Throne gives no intimation whatever of the intention of the government to consult the people of the country on its naval policy and the general question of a contribution by Canada to imperial defence. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) urges a plebiscite because he says the new policy of the government alters our relations with Great Britain. I may say at once that his reasons for a plebiscite do not commend themselves to me, and for my part I shall vote against his motion. There never was a referendum or a plebiscite in this country except in one instance to which I shall later refer. When Great Britain withdrew her military forces from Canada we assumed the defence of the country by a land force, and that certainly was a change in our constitutional position, but that change of policy was not submitted to the people. It was carried out by the Conservative government and the people were not consulted through a plebiscite. Then, we established a fishery protection service which was formerly provided for by Great Britain, and , that also caused a change in our constitutional position but the people were not consulted through a plebiscite. But far and above in importance either of these questions was the question of confederation, and let me ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) if that question, which was going to change the constitution not only in respect to our relations with Great Britain, but in respect to the interrelations between the provinces, w'as referred to the people? My hon. friend knows very well that it was not. It seems to me that if there wTas one case above all others which should have been referred to the people; if there was one question above all others upon which the people of Canada had a right to be consulted it was that policy of confederation.
The referendum, or plebiscite, is not in harmony with British constitutional practice. We have responsible government, we have a government of the people by the people, and if the government fails in its duty it may be overthrown to-morrow and a new government put in its place. In the United States the constitutional practice is different, because there the president and the congress is elected for a determined and a fixed period and it is their policy in some instances to submit important questions to the vote of the people. But, under the British system of parliamentary government the plebiscite is not in accordance with the constitutional principles and consequently it is not appealed to. And in ad-

dition to that, in my opinion it is very much better that the judgment of the people should be taken on such a question when the elections come on and then we will know exactly where we stand. Let me ask, if a plebiscite were taken on what would the people be asked _to pronounce themselves? Should we submit just the one question:	Are you in favour of the establishment of a Canadian naval service, or another question: Are you in favour of a contribution in money, or another question: Are you in favour of no naval service at all, as some people in Quebec contend for. Would we ask the people:	Are you in
favour of contributing to imperial defence and if so what form should that contribution take? I submit, Sir, that the policies of the different parties to this controversy are not so well defined that it would be possible to refer the matter to the people in a single and concrete question.
But we are not afraid of the judgment of the people ; on the contrary, we are in favour of consulting the people. There will be that consultation when the elections come on, and at that time the people will know exactly where they are. They will know, as they know to-day, the policy established by the government. They will know the policy of the Conservative party, which is the contribution policy. And I hope they will know the policy of the Nationalist party which we do not know to-day. These questions can be submitted to the people, but there are other questions which are not yet determined but which are under public discussion. And I say, let us have these questions discussed by the representatives of the people before the election comes on. If, on appeal to the people, it ibe found that our policy does not accord with public opinion, the people will have the right to reverse that policy. The people will be consulted in this way and will foe much better able to give their verdict than if the question had been submitted in the form of a plebiscite. As to this question of a plebiscite, my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) stated that a plebiscite had been asked for by
50.000	people. I do not know that there were that many, but, for the sake of argument, let us agree that there were 50,000. I know that the petition presented as coming from some parts of my own county was signed not only by electors but by women and by school children. And I am informed by my hon. friend from St. Johns (Mr. Demers) that there were not
50.000	who petitioned for a plebiscite, but only 27,188. But I base my calculation on
50,000,	so let us take that figure. Now, in the last election, there were 1,599,328 electors. If this plebiscite was asked for by
50.000	of the electors, that would mean that it was asked for by 3 per cent of the total number. But suppose we confine it
to the province of Quebec as the petitioners mainly reside in that province. In Quebec there are 414,428 electors and the actual number of petitioners was 27,000, which weuld be less than 7 per cent of the total. That being the case, would it be advisable, on a question on which the issues are not well determined, a question on which the policy of either party is not fully understood, to take a vote of the people? I say that it would be money spent uselessly to have a plebiscite under these circumstances. There was a plebiscite on prohibition, and we know with what result ; and I suppose we do not want to keep the people always in elections. Speaking for myself, this proposal of plebiscite does not commend itself to my judgment.
Our policy in this matter is an affirmation of our Canadian autonomy and an extension of our system of defence. Let me prove that it is an extension of our autonomy by comparing our present legislation with the legislation that, in 1865, we were authorized by the imperial parliament to pass. The Colonial Defence Act of 1865 provides as follows :
3. In any colony it shall be lawful for the proper legislative authority, with the approval of Her Majesty in Council, from time to time to make provision for effecting at the expense of the colony all or any of the purposes following:
(1)	For providing, maintaining, and using a vessel or vessels of war subject to such conditions and for such purposes as Her Majesty in Council from time to time approves;
(2)	For raising and maintaining seamen and others entered on the terms of being bound to serve as ordered in any such vessel;
(3)	For raising and maintaining a body of volunteers entered on the terms of being bound to general service in the Royal Navy in emergency, and, if in any case the proper legislative authority so directs, on the further terms of being bound to serve as ordered in any such vessel as aforesaid;
(4)	For appointing commissioned, warrant, and other officers to train and command or serve as officers with any such men, ashore or afloat, on such terms and subject to such regulations as Her Majesty in Council from time to time approves;
(5)	For obtaining from the Admiralty the services of commissioned, warrant, and of other officers and of men of the Royal Navy for the last mentioned purposes;
(6)	For enforcing good order and discipline among the men and officers aforesaid while ashore or afloat within the limits of the colony;
(7)	For making the men and officers aforesaid, while ashore or afloat within the limits of the colony or elsewhere, subj oct to all enactments and regulations for the time being in force for the discipline of the Royal Navy.
Two principles underlie this legislation of 1865. The first is that nothing can be



done except with the consent of the Imperial government. The second is that some of the men taking service in that navy would be obliged to join the Imperial navy in case of war, willing or unwilling. That was the situation in 1865 ; but what is it to-day? Are we obliged by the legislation that we have passed under the agreement that has been made to ask the consent of the Imperial government to establish vessels of war? No ; we have that freedom, and that freedom we are exercising to-day. And are those who volunteer in this naval service obliged to go into the Royal navy should war arise? No ; they, will be a Canadian naval reserve, which reserve will leave our coasts only with the consent of the Governor in Council and the approval of parliament. That is why I say that this legislation is an affirmation of our autonomy.
Now, I say that we must provide for a navy. The time has arrived when Canada must do something, first, for the defence of our coasts; second, for the protection of our commerce, and, third, for the maintenance of the naval supremacy of Great Britain. England has withdrawn her ships from our coasts. A few years ago there were naval stations on the Atlantic and the Pacific, at Esquimalt and Halifax, which were manned and equipped by officers of the British navy. But for reasons pertinent to the British Admiralty, Great Britain has withdrawn her ships from those coasts, and now there is not, on the coast of the maritime provinces, a single ship provided either for the defence of our coasts or for the protection of our commerce. The same may be said of the coast of British Columbia, with the exception of two small ships, the Algerine and Shearwater, which are not strong enough to make any effective defence in case of attack. I may say, moreover, that these ships in British Columbia are provided chiefly for the protection of the seal fisheries. A treaty exists between Great Britain and the United States by which pelagic sealing is prohibited during certain months of the year. This treaty was made in the interest of Canada, and for the protection of the pelagic sealing. Great Britain has, during the last few years, provided, at her own expense, the protection of these seal fisheries. There are, however, still some fisheries exercised exclusively by Canadian citizens, and surely it should be our duty to afford them protection, but Great Britain is still doing it for us. I say that the time has arrived when this protection should no longer be afforded by Great Britain, the time has arrived when Canada herself should protect her own seal fisheries. England having so much confidence in Canada, so much confidence in our resources, so much confidence in the loyalty of Canadians, has seen fit to transfer to us the two stations of Esquimalt and Halifax.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I think we should be proud of this attitude of Great Britain towards Canada in transferring to us those two naval stations. It seems to me we should be proud of the fact that to-day there is not one inch of land in Canada over which the Canadian government has not absolute control. Great Britain had enough confidence in our loyalty to transfer to us those two naval stations.
Now, hon. gentlemen opposite say, No, let us send warships to Great Britain, but let us not provide for the maintenace and equipment of those two naval stations. Sir, I differ from that view. I say that those stations having been transferred to us, and being now under our control, it is our duty to maintain them, it is our duty not only as citizens of Canada, but it is our duty under the treaty which exists to-day between Great Britain and Canada to maintain those naval stations and to keep them efficiently manned and equipped. That is the policy we are now carrying out, and it is a duty that we should not hesitate for a moment in performing. Great Britain is now affording no protection to our trade so far as the British Admiralty is concerned. Their vessels have been withdrawn and our shores are exposed to attack, not only in time of war, but even in time of peace. I say, therefore, it is our duty to protcet our trade routes, and that protection is required not only in time of war, but also in time of peace. Why do I say that? Why was the fishery protection service established? It was established because our fishery products were being taken away from us, because they were left without any protection, or without sufficient protection.
Now, it may be asked: What is the need of protecting our trade during time of peace? Do you fear pirates, do you fear robbers? Yes, Mr. Speaker, unfortunately pirates and robbers still infest the seas. Both on the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, and in the Gulf of Mexico, only last year there were cases where vessels were attacked by pirates. Let me quote some instances. I have in my hand an extract from Collier's, of October 15, 1910, which gives the history of the British vessel. The ' Princess May ' that went on the rocks a few days ago on the Pacific ocean. The history of this British vessel is given, and it is very interesting. The article mentions that though this vessel was built so recently as 1888, it has already been captured once by pirates, and again on another occasion was fiercely attacked. The article states that the ' Princess May ' was stolen from her berth at Shanghai by French adventurers, but she was relieved bv a Chinese warship and brought back. We see, therefore, what warships can do. A short time afterwards, while she was sailing on the Oriental coast, she was boarded by pirates, who surrounded her and almost gained possession of her. The battle

lasted many hours, the pirates were finally driven away, and to save themselves had to jump into the sea. Here is another case that occurred on the 25th of December, 1909. I read this from a newspaper published in the city of Ottawa :-

It was commanded by Captain F. A. McGorty and carried a crew of 14, all Philipinos.
The cutter left Salabo, 20 miles south of Palana, carrying J. L. Peary, collector of the port, who was bound to Sandakan in British North Borneo, to purchase supplies. Nothing has been heard the vessel 6ince.
I have also a statement here showing that a case of piracy occurred in the Gulf of Mexico last year. Here are four cases happening within a few years which show that merchant vessels are subject to attack by pirates and robbers, and I ask if under these conditions we shall leave our merchant marine and our products without protection. It is the duty of Canada to provide for the protection of their trade and that is what we are doing to-day in carrying out this policy.
Our naval policy should be continued for the purpose of assisting in maintaining the naval supremacy of Great Britain. We should all act with a common mind on this question. There is only one exception to this policy which has been heard in this House, and that exception was heard last night in the remarks that fell from the lips of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). He appears to be the only member of this House who goes to the length of declaring that we should do nothing in order to maintain the naval supremacy of Great Britain, and that we should not participate in the wars if that) naval supremacy should be threatened. The maintenance of the naval supremacy of Great Britain is essential to our trade and our freedom. I should say further that in the province of Quebec a sentiment in favour of such a policy should come from the gratitude that we owe to Great Britain for the freedom which she has given us. Quebec is most interested in maintaining this naval supremacy. It is interested, like other parts of the country, in maintaining the naval supremacy of Great Britain in order to protect our trade as I have just shown it needs protection. But besides that I would ask 6i
where would we be in the province of Quebec if the naval supremacy of Great Britain should be affected? What would become of our institutions? They despise the British flag. You will remember that last year in Rome, when the insurgents were taking possession of that city, alarm was felt for the safety of the Canadian college there, an institution where young seminarists from Montreal and other places go to continue their studies and to qualify themselves to become priests. When this insurrection broke out in Rome, what happened? The director of the institution, fearing that these insurgents would take possession of the college, put the British flag over the college in order to protect it against injury.
May I ask behind what flag the hon. gentleman and his friends ranged themselves in Drummond and Arthabaska?

We fought the campaign in Drummond and Arthabaska under the British flag. We fought that battle in Drummond and Arthabaska in resistance to all the racial appeals which were made against us. I stood there for the British flag. I stand to-day and I will always stand for the maintenance of the British flag. Now, I was giving you an instance where the British flag protected a Catholic institution last year in Rome. Just a few days ago there was a great revolution in Portugal, so serious that the king had to leave his throne, a change of government took place and republican institutions were established in place of the monarchy. What happened? There was a convent of monks, in which there were some British citizens. They feared for themselves, they feared that the new government, or the insurgents, would tear their convent to pieces. What did they do? They elevated the British flag on the institution, and in that way they maintained it against attack. I would not be surprised if some of those monks who were saved in that way were amongst those who, the other day, came to this country to enjoy the freedom which we enjoy so much under the British flag. I say that we have all the interest in the world in the province of Quebec to maintain the naval supremacy of Great Britain, and in spite of the prejudices to which appeals are made, I am sure that the people of Quebec will realize as we do that we should maintain our naval supremacy, not only for our material benefit, not only to continue the trade that we have established with Great Britain, but also to maintain the institutions that we have in the province of Quebec, and of which we are so proud.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier yesterday quoted the following paragraph from the Admiralty Memorandum which is con-

tamed in the blue-book ox the Eeport of the Imperial Defence Conference. Mr. McKenna, the First Lord of the Admiralty, in his memorandum dated 20th July, 1909, stated that:	[DOT]
It has been recognized by the colonial governments that in time of war the local naval forces should come under the general direction of the Admiralty.
The hon. gentleman has quoted that remark very often. He quoted it during the election, he quoted it last year and: I think even in an article which he published in Le'Devoir. He asks: Where is the, document that the Minister of Marine signed declaring that the Canadian government, in time of war, should put their forces under the general direction of the admiralty? He told to the electors by saying that they are afraid to show that document, they will not show it and there is a very good reason for that-so he said. Well, Mr. Speaker, I may inform my hon. friend that no such document exists. I have never signed any document either myself or in the name of the government or of my colleagues of such a nature. I may say besides that the statement of Mr. McKenna is made not in the conference, not as a result of the conference, but in a document dated the 20th July, 1909, while the conference only met on the 5th August, 1909. But, on what did Mr. McKenna base his declaration? I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) that Mr. McKenna based that declaration upon the statement which my hon. friend assented to when on the 29th of March, 1909, he voted for the famous resolution which has since attracted so much attention. Mr. McKenna made that statement on the declaration of the Prime Minister of New Zealand in his telegram of the 22nd of March, 1909; he made it on the declaration of the Prime Minister of Australia in a despatch of the 15th of April, 1909, and finally Mr. McKenna made that statement upon the declaration made by the member for Jacques Cartier himself on the 29th March, 1909. I think that disposes of the allegations which have been made in the Nationalist and Conservative press of the province of Quebec.
Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) has found another grievance against us, and he declares that the Canadian government has approved of the formation of an Imperial General Staff, which he seemed to think was a very dangerous thing. I shall quote authority as to what the Imperial General Staff is, and then thei House will understand that my hon. friend need not feel very great alarm. Had the hon. gentleman taken the trouble to consult the report of the proceedings of' the conference of 1907 he would have known what the Imperial General Staff Mr. BRODEUR.
is,	but the moment he saw the word>
'Imperial' he thought it was his duty to' denounce the whole thing and to condemnj the Canadian government. Let me quote from page 119 of the report of the conference of 1907 what the Imperial Gen-< eral Staff is:-
The conference without wishing to commit to immediate action any of the governments represented, as it recognizes and affirms the need of developing a general staff recruited from the forces of the empire as a whole which should be a- means of fostering the study of military science in the various branches.
That is very serious is'nt it. There is going to be a staff composed of officers from Great Britain and New Zealand and Australia and Canada and these men, are going to foster the study of military science. What an alarming thing:-
They shall collect and disseminate te the various governments military information and intelligence.
Is there anything very treasonable in that? The resolution continues:-
And undertake the preparation of schemes of defence on a common principle and without in the least interfering in questions connected with command and administration.
Is that so very serious?
And shall at the request of the respective governments advise them as to the training education and war organization of the military forces of the Crown in every part of the empire.
There we have a declaration as to what the Imperial General Staff is, and yet that does not prevent my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) going to the province of Quebec and stating: Look at this order in council; they are creating an Imperial General Staff, they are creating a staff imperial in its nature. I think, Mr. Speaker, that this will show that the appeals made by these gentlemen opposite are not' founded on reason. When, we seek to got) at the true facts we see that in every case-this government has preserved that principle ;of autonomy under which we have been living for so many years.
I think I have answered most of the points raised by my hon. friend and I regret that I have wearied the House by speaking at such length. We are in Canada face to face with the problem of naval service. Like most of the military expenditures, the expenditures for naval service do not command much favour among certain classes in Canada. But, members of parliament should fully recognize the duty of our country in that respect. Public men should be aware that the country requires to be protected against aggression and that the government which does not provide

for such defence is derelict in its duty. In all countries enjoying the benefits of parliamentary institutions and of party governments, the question of defence is sacred, and no one who properly measures his sense of responsibility would dare to bring military organization into contempt and discredit. We have hitherto adhered to that principle in this country so far as our military expenditure is concerned, and whether Liberals or Conservatives were in power criticism has been offered in such a way as not to afford much comfort to the anti-military element. The creation of a naval service has given rise to the most unfair criticism. Appeals have been made to those who deprecate military expenditure and all sorts of misrepresentations have been resorted to in order to create prejudice. Not satisfied with that anti-national conduct, appeals have also been made to racial prejudice. In Ontario and Manitoba the policy of the government has been attacked because it was anti-British, and in the province of Quebec, it has been attacked because our opponents said it was a pro-British policy. We were accused in Quebec of having sacrificed our country although we provided that in case of war, with the consent and the approval oi parliament, our ships should form part of the Royal navy. The charges made against us are absolutely unfounded and unfair, and they are not made by men who wish to see our country discharge its duty properly and effectively. However, Mr. Speaker, we are not scared by these frantic appeals; we stand by our policy and we will fall with it if the people so decide.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the House in English I feel that I must ask your indulgence. I would not dare to make such an attempt were it not my strongest desire to be understood by every hon. gentleman in this House. In spite of all the statements published in the newspapers and made in this House to the contrary, I declare from my seat in parliament, and I declare in the face of my fellow-countrymen that during the whole campaign in Drummond and Arthabaska we who spoke in opposition to the government candidate remained loyal and faithful to our King, to our country, and to what we think are the true principles of the Liberal Conservative party.
Ha, ha.

Let me say Tight here, Mr. Speaker, that I take to myself no credit or discredit by my presence in Drummond and Arthabaska for the result of that contest, because I may say that before I ever went into the constituency, and before any of my friends ever went into the constituency the people had made up their minds
to vote against the Navy Bill. I myself have heard organizers and friends of hon. gentlemen opposite saying that things were working, badly in Drummond and Arthabaska because of what they called ' this dam Naval Bill.' I am particularly grateful to my hon. friends opposite when they attempt, on false reports of newspapers, to represent me as having said that French Canadians do not care about the opinions of the other provinces on this naval question. These are not exactly my words, but I said something in that sense, and this is how it came. Our friends opposite tried to make the people of Drummond and Arthabaska fear to express their free will on this question, representing that if they did so the other provinces would retaliate upon them. They tried to make the people of Drummond and Arthabaska believe that the people of the English provinces were narrowminded and fanatical; and it was because of those statements that I told 'my fellow-citizens not to be afraid of the English provinces. Some of our friends opposite said to the people of Drummond and Arthabaska that all we are and all we have we owe to Great Britain, and I answered, with Sir Charles Tupper, with Sir Richard Cartwright, and with many of the members of this House who sit at your right, Mr. Speaker, that it was untrue.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the statements of newspapers are not the only ones which are false. I think the hon. minister who has just addressed the Hotise (Hon. Mr. Bro-deur) fell a victim of those false statements himself when he referred to a certain cartoon which he said had been distributed in Drummond and Arthabaska. He said:-
Then, there were cartoons distributed throughout the county by these Nationalists. One of them I hold in my hand. Of course, to them the British flag was nothing, if it should be trampled upon. This little cartoon, however, shows what kind of spirit there is in this Conservative party of the province elf Quebec. It represents Baptiste smoking liis pipe quietly and holding the Union Jack with both hands. Behind him is the Britisher, John Bull. Baptiste has taken off his coat and hung it on a tree, and the Britisher says to him : 'Hold the flag Baptiste, and while you are doing that I will take care of your coat.'
That cartoon, with its inscription, Mr. Speaker, never originated in the minds of Nationalists. It is a child of the hon. minister himself. It is not a picture of ' le Nationalist.' It is a reproduction of a picture published_by ' Le Canada,' and on the newspaper which, the minister had in his hand were words which should have advised him of that fact. Mr. Speaker, I will not take up the time of the House by reading quotations: but as an example of newspaper reports, let me make a short quotation from the Brockville ' Evening Recorder,' which is, I believe, the organ of one of the minis-

ters. In its issue of the 19th of November it says:-
Yesterday's performance was looked forward * PL1 t interest as the new member from Arthabaska was to be present. This Nationalist arrived and as a general rule great applause heralds the entrance of a new victor, but the silence which greeted him was only equalled when Mr. Monk took his seat.
The hon, Minister of Marine and Fisheries stated that the cartoon just referred to and another one were circulated in Drummond and Arthabaska during the campaign. The hon. gentleman is wrong again. If he will look -at the newspaper from which he took the cartoon he will see that it was published three days after the election. Let me quote from a speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Marine of himself in 1896 in this House, when he was voting against the militia supply. What did he say of England on that occasion? He said:-
We have over and again been told that in the event of a war taking place or Canada being invaded, we could rely on Great Britain's pro-tectiou ; and. tliat tlie only ground for not severing the colonial tie was that, should international difficulties arise, we might rely on England s strong arm. Now, Sir, I am sorry to hear under the circumstances that the government, for the purpose of arming the Canadian militia have made their purchases, not from private contractors, but from the War Office in Great Britain, and that we are asked now to foot the bills. Is that the protection we have been promised by Great Britain? Is that the position in which we stand as a colony? I think we are entitled to an altogether different treatment at the hands of Great Britain.
In the campaign in Drummond and Arthabaska, hon. gentlemen opposite repeated their old speeches on the Riel question, and the Manitoba school question, in which they appealed to race prejudice. They have been brought up on that policy, and in my province since they have been in power they have tried to exploit the race cry as much as they could. Our first reason for fighting this Naval Bill in Drummond and Arthabaska is that it constitutes a menace to the existing relations between Great Britain and Canada, and I stated everywhere that we were ready to give our lives for the protection of our country and the continuance of British supremacy. I shall not speak any longer on this question. All I wanted to do was to explain my position, and before taking my seat I desire to register my protest in the name of the electors of Drummond and Arthabaska and on behalf of the whole province of Quebec against my hon. friends opposite when they endeavour to make us, this House and country believe that the people of the province of Quebec -are unable to judge a question fairly, but are so easily influenced by race cries and prejudices. In spite, Sir, of racial cries, the province of Quebec gave its support to the late Sir John

i
Macdonald during 18 years, and when the proper time comes the people of the province of Quebec will show the country that they can make up their minds on public questions apart f?om any consideration of nationality and give their support to an Englishman just as well as to a French Canadian.

I did not intend taking any part in this debate, but after the explanation which my hon. friend from Champlain (Mr. Blondin) has seen fit to offer in excuse for his conduct in the counties of Drummond and Arthabaska, I find it my duty to say a few words in that connection. My hon. friend must have considered himself guilty, and very much so, when he was compelled to seek an excuse in the past history of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec especially with regard to school questions. But we must all have noticed that my hon. friend (Mr. Blondin) did not deny squarely and flatly the statement made last night by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) to the effect that he had used during the last election language which could be qualified as disloyal. I noticed last night that when the hon. gentleman was accused of having given expression to some disloyal utterances at one of the meetings at Victoriaville, he replied : I do not deny that that was said but it was not said by me. The House will be rather amused, I am sure, to learn that at that meeting there were only two men who spoke on the Nationalist's side, one of whom was my hon. friend, and the other one was the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Paquet). Therefore if the one be -not guilty, the other is. I think that the House and the country fully realize that most-improper and disloyal language was used all through the last campaign by speakers on behalf of the Nationalist candidate. That cannot be denied.
Coming to my hon. friend the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), he laid very much stress on the work of organization which had been carried on during that election, and even before the election, by the Liberal party, and he did this in order to demonstrate how important was the victory the Nationalists had won.
I propose in a very few words to try and give the House the main features of the campaign. Let me say, in the first place, that the candidate elected, presented himself as a Liberal and a friend of the Liberal administration. At West Wickham I was alone with a law student, while there were against us both members for Ba.got, two lawyers from Quebec, and one from Montreal, which I need not mention. Here, then, is the hon. member making an exaggeration on this point as he had made many others.
Mr. Speaker, do you know how the election was carried? As I have said a moment ago, we did not fear to strike on the head of the government with respect to his naval policy. We have especially attacked his candidate. Here is a point which has not been dealt with, so far; but I am going to speak about it.
The government's candidate is a refined man, a perfect gentleman, an eloquent lawyer, but he had against him the fact of having given his opinion a little too soon on this question of a navy. As early as 1902, at Victoriaville, on St. Jean Baptiste day, a resolution was adopted approving the anti-imperialist policy of the right honourable Prime Minister, then in London, for the intercolonial conference and which contained amongst other things, this paragraph: "We do not wish to make the bonds which unite Canada with the British Empire, any tighter than they are, or to assume towards the empire any obligations more onerous than those imposed by the constitution of Canada and which Great Britain has declared herself satisfied with.' And they also asked: ' That the present resolution be transmitted to the hon. Prime Minister,' then in London, as I have just said. That resolution was proposed by Mr. Perreault, the government's candidate in the last election, seconded by Mr. Tourigny, the local member, and I have used it as one of the best arguments in that electoral contest. I said' ' Look at Mr. Perreault, the government's candidate; he was anti-imperialist in 1902, and consequently against the navy; he approved his anti-imperialist chieftain, and he now agrees to all that which that same chieftain has just done, especially the navy; he is ready aforehand to vote with his chief in spite of anything.' I think that argument had more weight than those so-called arguments mentioned a moment ago by the hon. member for Beauce and tending to show the poor boys being taken away from their mothers' bosom for future "wars. I have seen nobody, either, running from house to house under the pretense of taking the census and of taking the names of the children in every family.
(Translation.) I wish to call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that I did not speak of children who were to be ripped open; it is Mr. Bourassa who said that at Grand'Mere.

(Translation.) Nobody will make me believe that it is possible to awe an intelligent population as that of Drummond-Arthabaska, by sending so-called enumerators to take the names of the family heads and their children in the course of an electoral contest. It is very well for one to say such things after he has lost an election, after he has won but a moral victory; but nobody will take any

stock in such sayings. I think, really, that giving to suppose the French Canadians so candid as to accept such stupidities is to depreciate them in the other provinces and in the eyes of the other races.
Hon. ' JACQUES BUREAU. (Translation.) But, meanwhile, you tried to make them swallow those stupidities.
(Translation.) Somebody has mentioned the name of Jean Prevost, I believe?
(Translation.) Yes.

(Translation.) You may rest at ease. He has crossed the Rubicon about this naval question, and I do not think you will ever have the advantage of seeing him in your ranks again.
But let us return to the question. Mr. La-vergne wTas made a senator, and immediately the election took place within the space of a few days. I heard it said by the member for Beauce, a moment ago, that should the ministerialists have had ten or fifteen days more, they would have carried the election. Well, should we have three or four days more previous to the polling day, your candidate would have been defeated by a majority not of 200 but of 500. In fact, things went better and better for us every day; our voters were brought to the polls for us by your own canvassers. I am aware that at West Wickham the government party had two or three so-called hay dealers, who remained there from the Sunday preceding until polling day. However, it strikes me that dairy farmers would be more in the case of buying hay than of selling any. On polling day these gentlemen brought the voters to the polling booth, while the latter voted against the government candidate, so much so, that about three o'clock there were no more hay dealers in sight, they having lost all hope, no doubt.
As stated previously, as a rule, in the course of that election, friends directed their shafts straight at the leader of the government. In reply to the fiery appeals which were indulged in at every meeting in connection with that great man's name, working on race _ sympathies, stating: A vote for Gilbert is a vote against Laurier; it will mean the murder of that great French Canadian,-and these good people -who aTe thorough peace-lovers, could hardly believe it, -we cried out: Do not believe anything of the sort, gentlemen; the result wili have no such effect on him; only he will probably be more cautious in the future.
As regards myself, I confess having said: Your great man to whom some would look to as to a god, for the last fifteen years, is only a mortal man. He is a man swayed like all others by the necessities and appetites of human nature; a man who is at times accepting gifts and titles, after having strongly condemned the practice. After Mr! NANTEL.
taunting his opponents for accepting gifts, he has allowed his Finance Minister to accept $120,000 from his friends. I, for one, have never had the advantage of receiving such donations. If I were Prime Minister or Minister of Finance, I might be favoured with the gift of an automobile. Your hero is a great Canadian, I admit it, but he is still human.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: (Translation.) That is your reason for fighting the Navy Bill?

(Translation.) I do not think it necessary to answer such a query. Well, I repeat it, that was the general trend of our argument. In regard to conscription, we did not deceive the people; we were frank enough to put things in their true light. I, for one, stated that conscription was not compulsory under the statute, neither in Canada or in England, but that a time might come when it would be compulsory in Great Britain. That view was expounded down there, and it was stated that if Great Britain wished to keep her own against Germany, compulsory service would have to be enacted. And I added that if Great Britain went in for military conscription and called on the Prime Minister to enforce it in Canada, the latter would consent to it, in the same way that he agreed to send contingents to South Africa, after refusing to do so, and in the same way that he agreed to building a navy after fighting imperialism the greater part of his life.
Sir, if the election lasted only a fortnight, who is to blame? Possibly myself. The hon. Minister of Marine contended yesterday that I was responsible if a translation into French of the report of the Imperial Conference in regard to defence was no longer issued, because, he said that is a matter dealt with by the Printing Committee (of which I am a member). But it should not be forgotten that the powers that be make up their committees in such a way that their opponents may not be in a majority or take the lead under any circumstances. I shall accordingly free myself of all responsibility in this connection.
I believe it is some part of the policy of our opponents to hold the opposition responsible for anything that may occur. That is the stand they take in regard to the Printing Bureau scandal. It is the statute that is all wrong, they say. These gentlemen have been in power since 1896, and if the Act is defective and the Bureau badly managed, they have not been able to find out in the meantime, and have made no changes or improvements.
If the election has been put through in such a short time, a fortnight, it was not with a view to favouring the opposition. The government supporters were made aware of the date of the election before their oppon-

ents were apprised of it; so that it was rather laudable to see the government candidate at a meeting at Wickham complain that he would hardly have enough time to go around the various localities. However, that shortness of the campaign turned out to be in his favour, for if we only had had a few days more before polling day the majority against his return would have reached the 500 mark instead of the 200.
(Translation.) Why not say that your candidate would have been returned by acclamation?

(Translation.) If our candidate was not returned by acclamation, it is no fault of the Solicitor General. I have not met him, but if my information is correct, during the contest he took things very coolly; no doubt he expected that things would turn out that way.
But the verdict of the people does not carrv much meaning for these gentlemen. No doubt they will not pay any more heed to it than to the protests which were voiced in the course of the last session, or to the petitions asking for a referendum signed by
21,000	people, according to the figures given by the Minister of Marine. The intention is now to appeal from the decision of the people wrongly informed to that of the people better informed by means of an educational campaign. No doubt, it is to open that campaign that the Prime Minister sent that first pastoral letter to ' La l'resse.' But to the teacher of 1910, propounded imperialism and the establisment of a war navy, it will be sufficient to oppose the wisdom of that same teacher in 1896, condemning openly ot indirectly the purchase of rifles, or in 1902 and 1907 arguing before the Intercolonial Conference at London against imperialism. And one sure thing, the educator of 1896, Wilfrid Laurier, was more in touch with the popular feeling than the educator of 1910.
I shall not dilate any longer on this question. It is well understood that our policy is not one of inactivity, and it is not inactivity to develop our country where things await development at every point. I believe that heretofore we have done our share. It should be borne in mind that Canada is not an old country settled for many centuries past and fully equipped in all respects.
If the government came out openly before the people with the Naval Bill, and if the people approve of such a Bill, the province of Quebec would submit to the wish of the majority and would do her share, I am satisfied. She would not oppose the will of the majority of the Canadian people. But we contend that, in regard to this question, the province of Quebec is not alone in holding this view; the people in the other provinces are of the same opinion and we think it necessary to know what are
the views of the people as a whole on this question.
Even in the course of this debate, an effort is made to brand us as disloyal subjects. It is not worth while answering such charges; I am satisfied that the English speaking people who are of a practical and clear mind, have sized up the situation, [DOT]barring some newspaper men who are not acquainted with us, have never visited the province of Quebec, and write at random things which can only cause a shrugging of the shoulders.
In conclusion, I wish to dispel all misunderstanding in regard to the province of Quebec. If the majority of the whole people decide against what we consider the wise and right policy to follow for Canada, the province, of Quebec will do her share, and for my part I shall loyally submit and contribute. However, I believe that it would better ensure the permanency and durability of that policy to consult the people beforehand, and I shall vote in favour of the amendment of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier.
Mr. JOSEPH TURCOTTE (Quebec) (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, it appears that, during this last recess of parliament an election has taken place, and that as a result the government candidate was defeated. There is nothing in such a fact to be much wondered at. Following on the first session of the present parliament a vacancy occurred in the representation and a byelection took place in the county of Montcalm. On that occasion as well, the government candidate was defeated; but the successful candidate took his seat on the government side, and is to-day one of the staunchest supporters of the government's policy. Nevertheless, hon. gentle-ment opposite were not remiss, when the outcome of the election in Montcalm was made known, in boasting that they had scored a victory over the government.
Such defeats are facts, incidents, which occur now and then and which should not cause much surprise, having sometimes a meaning, w'hile at other times they signify nothing. A few years ago an election took place in Quebec county, for the purpose of replacing the gentleman who is to-day Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada. The government had their candidate in that election; the opposition had theirs. The government candidate was beaten. What happened then? For two sessions this House had the advantage, the pleasure, if I may so term it, of having within its precincts a sample of Canadian nationalism. And what happened next? At the general election of 1908, that same nationalist who had been elected to protest against the general policy of the government was defeated in the same constituency.

It is asserted that history repeats itself. Why should it not repeat itself in Drum-mond-Arthabaska on the same lines as in the county of Quebec? General elections will he forthcoming and the electors of Drum-mond-Arthabaska will ibe called upon once more to express an opinion. Now, is there any one in this House who would dare assert that the outcome in that constituency during a general election will be the same as it was the other day?
A by-election is not a consultation on the general policy of the government. Hence, it cannot be contended that the electors of Drummond-Arthabaska have taken a stand on the fiscal policy of the government, or as regards their general policy, for instance, regarding agriculture. A single note has been sounded, a note of fear. War has been mentioned, the scarecrow of desolation and ruin has been exhibited, and by working on the prejudices of the people, our opponents have succeeded in stampeding public opinion in the constituency.
I challenge any of those who have taken part in the fray in favour of the successful candidate to say that they have touched on a single issue of the government's general policy other than the naval question.
(Translation.) I have done so.
(Translation.) On what questions?

(Translation.) On questions of general policy.
Mr. TURCOTTE'. (Translation.) What
questions? The hon. member claims he has taken exception to the government's policy but he is unable to recall what questions he dealt with.
This is not the time to discuss that naval question. It was threshed out last year. The Act is in force ; to-day it is the law of the country. It was voted in accordance with the mandate which the House issued on March 29, 1909, The opposition themselves as well as the supporters of the government, all representing the popular will, following on a general consultation, have approved of that resolution of March 29, 1909.
We are the trustees of the people, and it is the people's representatives who unanimously voted that resolution without a single protest from any one. That resolution was based on the same principle which underlies the Naval Service Act now in force. Consequently, there is no reason for taking up that question once more. We are discussing the speech from the Throne, and the question is what answer the House of Commons wishes to forward.
Mr. Speaker, I have read that speech of Mr. TURCOTTE.
the representative of His Majesty. I have read it over with care. I heard members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition criticise some of the public acts, or some of the methods of the government, whether as regards past measures, whether as regards measures presently to be submitted to the House, that concerning a treaty of reciprocity, for instance. That is a discussion worthy of the representatives of the people in this House. But, furthermore I noticed another bone of contention; I heard the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, and his colleagues present their case. How is it that these gentlemen do not dare discuss the general policy of the government? They have referred to a single matter: a passing victory scored by means which they themselves admit as having been suspicious. Have these gentlemen resolved on restricting the discussion to that sole issue? Is it their intention to develop here a feeling similar to that which they have succeeded in developing in a constituency of the province of Quebec?
Well, though not a prophet, I think I may predict that in this House they will meet with the same humiliation as when they proposed a sub-amendment to the Naval Bill. They were, as we had occasion to notice only a small group, and they remained such. Through sympathy a few English-speaking members on the other side of the House, joined in with those who proposed forming a separatist party in the Dominion. I trust, I am satisfied that those who followed them at the time will abandon them to-day, and that this group of seventeen of last session will be considerably reduced; for we are not here to represent not factions, or prejudices, or antinational and unpatriotic feelings. We are here as trustees of the people to expedite public business, not only in matters of pecuniary interest, not only with a view to developing the resources of that great Dominion, which has been designated a nation; but moreover-since we are considered as being an elite among the people whom we represent-to point out to them an ideal. That ideal which it is our purpose to show to the people, should not be confined to one section of the country; that ideal is the love of all that makes up one's fatherland. The love of country should not be confused with those common place cravings which are easily satisfied; it is a feeling of a superior kind which induces us to look beyond the present into the misty future, and makes for the happiness of the land of our birth and which one day \yill contain our grave.
We have the right and it is our duty to carrj on the debate in this House on a higher plane than that of the prejudices which are interwoven into human nature, a nature, in itself, not always superexcellent. It is incumbent on us to see to it that these

differences do not become too marked. We should endeavour to put an end to that unfortunate spirit of pugnacity which is at the bottom of our nature, but which may be held in check or counteracted by education.
Should this working on the prejudices of the people be allowed to continue, it may result in bringing about, even in connection with material interests a conflict of which, once it is started we may never see the end.
The hon. member for Terrebonne referred to Mr. Jean Prevost, who was his opponent and he stated that he had crossed the Rubicon. Were I to take his words literally, I believe I would be doing an injustice to the hon. member, for they have not only been political enemies, but have at the same time been separated by clan differences, clans which have waged war on one another in pursuance, I might say, of family traditions. If I were to consult past history in order to foresee future events, I would say that this is an inauspicious alliance, the mere outcome of circumstances. A party cannot be made up of individuals who abandon their leaders, who desert the flag. A party made up of deserters cannot be a party of patriots, a government party. Deserters should not be expected to work for the good of the country, or in the public interest.
Mr. Speaker, as a rule, the speech from the Throne and the debate which ensues as carried on by the leaders of both parties, is a preliminary discussion. I understand that the various proposals therein mentioned will be further looked into by the House. We will then have a better insight into the motives which inspire hon. members who have already spoken on the address. We will then also find out what are the motives which will prompt the utterances and votes of the member whom these gentlemen have caused to be returned for Drummond and Arthabaska.
If it be true, as I have heard it stated often times, that this election has been the outcome of false representations, we shall witness in this House strange things, but which I can foretell without being a prophet, and it is this: if the naval question is brought up once more, though it is not likely to be, then the member elect for Drummond and Arthabaska will possibly cast his vote with those who brought about his return. But, in regard to any other question, if he be a man of honour-and I hope he is-if he is man to stick to his word-and I trust he is-lastly, if he is a true Canadian-and I know he is, for he belongs to the great farming community-he will vote in accordance with the pledges he has given, and in that case the member for Drummond and Arthabaska, will give us a second exhibition of what we saw when the 7
member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) was returned: he will vote with us.
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take a hand in the debate at this stage of the session. I have done so, because I heard it stated, and the rumor was. current, that I had deserted my party to-join, not an honourable party, but the so-called nationalist party. Thank God, as long as I have the honour to represent a county such as the county of Quebec, I shall not be seen deserting the ranks of the liberal party to join a party of deserters.
PAQUET, (L'Islet), (Translation): Mr. Speaker, after this long sitting, I shall, if the right hon. gentleman will allow me to do so, move the adjournment of the debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am quite willing.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
House adjourned at six o'clock.

Thursday, November 24, 1910.
